question: Nico controls Analia's [Bane Alley Blackguard] enchanted with their [Corrupted Conscience]. Analia casts their own [Lay Claim], targeting Nico's Corrupted Conscience. After it resolves, who controls the Bane Alley Blackguard? Who controls the Corrupted Conscience?
answer:
After Analia's Lay Claim resolves, Analia controls all three permanents: Lay Claim, Corrupted Conscience, and Analia's Bane Alley Blackguard.

Why: Lay Claim reads "Enchant permanent / You control enchanted permanent," and Corrupted Conscience is itself a permanent (an Aura enchantment), so it's a legal target. Once Lay Claim is attached, Analia becomes the controller of Corrupted Conscience — an Aura's controller is tracked separately from what it's attached to (rule 303.4e).

Corrupted Conscience says "You control enchanted creature." The word "you" on an Aura means that Aura's controller, which is now Analia. Control-changing effects are all applied together in layer 2 (rule 613.1b), and within that layer the effect of Corrupted Conscience now grants control to Analia rather than Nico. So Bane Alley Blackguard goes back to Analia — who also happens to be its owner and its default controller (rule 110.2). Nico keeps nothing from this arrangement.

Note the general principle in the Lay Claim ruling: gaining control of a creature does not give you the Auras on it, and an Aura's "you" always refers to the Aura's own controller. Here Analia used that principle in reverse — instead of taking the creature, she took the Aura that grants control of the creature, and the creature followed.

Bane Alley Blackguard remains enchanted by Corrupted Conscience, so it still has infect. This works the same whether the game has exactly two players or more; no multiplayer-specific rule changes the outcome (control questions would only shift if a player left the game, per rule 800.4a).

answer_gold: Analia controls both permanents. Out of the two auras, Corrupted Conscience has the earlier timestamp, and would normally be applied first. The Lay Claim's effect applies first, giving Analia control of Corrupted Conscience, and then the Corrupted Conscience's effect applies, giving Analia control of Bane Alley Blackguard.

question: Alan controls [Iroas, God of Victory] and 3 other enchantments. Their devotion to white is 2. They cast [Starfield of Nyx]. After it resolves, is Iroas, God of Victory a creature? If so, what are its power and toughness?
answer:
Yes — after Starfield of Nyx resolves, Iroas, God of Victory is a creature, and it's a 4/4.

Why:

1. Enchantment count: Alan controls Iroas, God of Victory, 3 other enchantments, and Starfield of Nyx itself = five enchantments, so Starfield of Nyx's ability is active. Iroas, God of Victory is a non-Aura enchantment other than Starfield of Nyx, so it's affected.

2. Type-changing (layer 4): Iroas, God of Victory's own ability says "As long as your devotion to red and white is less than seven, Iroas isn't a creature." Devotion to red and white counts every red and/or white mana symbol among the mana costs of permanents Alan controls [700.5a]; with devotion to white only 2, the combined total is well under seven, so that ability is trying to remove the creature type. Starfield of Nyx says the enchantment "is a creature in addition to its other types." Both effects apply in layer 4, and within a layer effects apply in timestamp order [613.1, 613.6, 613.4a]. Starfield of Nyx entered the battlefield later, so its effect is applied after Iroas, God of Victory's, and the final result is that Iroas, God of Victory is a creature (an enchantment creature).

3. Power/toughness (layer 7b): Starfield of Nyx sets "base power and base toughness each equal to its mana value." Iroas, God of Victory's mana cost is {2}{R}{W}, mana value 4, so its base power and toughness become 4/4, replacing the printed 7/4 [302.4c, 613.1g, 613.4a]. With no other pump effects, counters, or anchor-word effects mentioned, it's a 4/4 indestructible Legendary Enchantment Creature — God.

Timing note: I'm assuming Starfield of Nyx has the later timestamp (it just entered). If instead an effect gave Iroas, God of Victory's non-creature ability a later timestamp, it would be applied after Starfield of Nyx and Iroas, God of Victory would not be a creature — though the layer-7b power/toughness setting effect would still exist and simply do nothing while it isn't a creature [208.3a].

Multiplayer note: nothing here changes with player count; devotion only counts permanents Alan controls.

question: Alex activates [Inkmoth Nexus] to turn it into a creature and attacks Nadia with it. Nadia doesn't block it and then casts [Summoning Trap], putting [Melira, Sylvok Outcast] onto the battlefield. What happens during the combat damage step?
answer:
Inkmoth Nexus loses infect, so it deals 1 normal combat damage to Nadia and she loses 1 life — no poison counter.

Why: Melira, Sylvok Outcast reads "Creatures your opponents control lose infect" and "You can't get poison counters." Inkmoth Nexus is a creature Alex controls (a 1/1 Phyrexian Blinkmoth artifact creature with flying and infect until end of turn), and Alex is Nadia's opponent, so once Melira, Sylvok Outcast is on the battlefield Inkmoth Nexus no longer has infect. Melira, Sylvok Outcast's ability has the later timestamp here (the animation of Inkmoth Nexus happened first), so it wins ([Melira, Sylvok Outcast ruling #1]).

Timing assumption: Summoning Trap resolved and Melira, Sylvok Outcast entered before the combat damage step began. That matters because replacement/prevention-style and damage-result effects are not locked in ahead of time — they're checked as the damage event happens [614.1] [615.1] [120.4b] [120.4c]. So when combat damage is dealt as a turn-based action in the combat damage step [510.1] [510.2] [703.4k] [703.4m], the 1 damage from Inkmoth Nexus is ordinary damage: it causes Nadia to lose 1 life rather than giving a poison counter [120.2a] [120.3] [702.90b].

If instead Melira, Sylvok Outcast somehow arrived after combat damage was already dealt, the poison counter would already have been given — but note that no player gets priority between damage assignment and damage being dealt [510.2], so there is no window inside the combat damage step to sneak Melira, Sylvok Outcast in.

Belt and suspenders: even if Inkmoth Nexus had kept infect, Melira, Sylvok Outcast's "You can't get poison counters" would stop the poison counter, and Nadia would simply not lose life either — the damage would have no result at all, though damage-triggered abilities would still see it [Melira, Sylvok Outcast ruling #1] [702.90b].

This works the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table: the only thing that matters is that Alex is an opponent of Melira, Sylvok Outcast's controller, Nadia, and that Nadia is the player being dealt damage.

question: Nathaniel controls a [Melira, Sylvok Outcast]. Ari activates [Inkmoth Nexus] to turn it into a creature and attacks Nathaniel with it. Nathaniel doesn't block. What happens during the combat damage step?
answer:
Nathaniel takes 1 combat damage from Inkmoth Nexus, but nothing happens: he doesn't lose life and he doesn't get a poison counter.

Why: Melira, Sylvok Outcast says "Creatures your opponents control lose infect" and "You can't get poison counters." Inkmoth Nexus's own activated ability grants it infect when it resolves, which is a later timestamp than Melira, Sylvok Outcast's static ability, so the most recent effect wins and Inkmoth Nexus does have infect while attacking [Melira, Sylvok Outcast ruling #1] [Inkmoth Nexus].

Step by step: Inkmoth Nexus is unblocked, so it assigns its combat damage (1, equal to its power) to the player it's attacking, Nathaniel [510.1b] [120.2a]; that damage is then dealt simultaneously as a turn-based action with no priority in between [510.2] [703.4m]. Because the source, Inkmoth Nexus, has infect, the damage doesn't cause Nathaniel to lose life; instead it would give him a poison counter [702.90b] [120.3b]. Melira, Sylvok Outcast stops him from getting poison counters, so when the damage is processed into its results, no counter is given and no life is lost [120.4c] [Melira, Sylvok Outcast ruling #1].

Note that the damage was still dealt: abilities that trigger on damage being dealt (lifelink, "whenever this deals damage to a player" triggers) would still see it [120.4b] [Melira, Sylvok Outcast ruling #1]. Also, Melira, Sylvok Outcast doesn't remove poison counters Nathaniel already has [Melira, Sylvok Outcast ruling #0].

Multiplayer: the same result holds. In a game with more than two players, combat damage is assigned in APNAP order but the step otherwise works identically [802.5]; Melira, Sylvok Outcast only protects its own controller, so if Ari attacked a different opponent with Inkmoth Nexus, that player would get a poison counter normally.

question: Autumn controls [Painter's Servant] naming "blue" and [Sword of Body and Mind]. Nico casts [Gift of Tusks] targeting the Painter's Servant. After it resolves, what happens if Autumn tries to equip Painter's Servant with Sword of Body and Mind?
answer:
The equip works. Sword of Body and Mind attaches to Painter's Servant, which becomes a 5/5 green Elephant (base 3/3 from Gift of Tusks, plus +2/+2) with protection from green and from blue.

Why nothing stops it:

1. Gift of Tusks makes Painter's Servant lose all abilities, so its "All cards that aren't on the battlefield, spells, and permanents are the chosen color" ability is gone (113.10 — effects can remove abilities). Sword of Body and Mind is therefore just a colorless artifact Equipment again, not blue.
2. Equip is "[Cost]: Attach this permanent to target creature you control. Activate only as a sorcery" (702.6a). Painter's Servant is still a creature Autumn controls (a green Elephant), so it's a legal target, and an Equipment may legally be attached to any creature (301.5c).
3. The protection from green and from blue only exists once Sword of Body and Mind is attached, and Sword of Body and Mind itself is neither green nor blue, so the state-based action in 702.16d (a permanent with protection can't be equipped by Equipment with the stated quality, and such Equipment becomes unattached) does not fire. Protection from green also never protects Painter's Servant from its own green color in any relevant way here.

Timing caveat worth acting on: Gift of Tusks lasts only until end of turn. When it wears off during the cleanup step, Painter's Servant regains its ability and (with blue already chosen) makes all permanents blue, including Sword of Body and Mind. At that point the equipped creature has protection from blue from a blue Equipment, so 702.16d's state-based action (704.1 — state-based actions happen automatically and don't use the stack) unattaches Sword of Body and Mind, which stays on the battlefield. If instead Autumn tries to activate equip after Gift of Tusks has already worn off, the ability can still be activated and resolve, but Sword of Body and Mind will immediately fall off the same way.

Also note the general precedence rule: if some other effect said Painter's Servant "can't be equipped," that "can't" would win (101.2a) — but no such effect is present here. Player count doesn't matter: equip targets a creature its controller controls, so the answer is the same in a two-player or multiplayer game.

question: Nathanael controls [Grizzly Bears] and [Muraganda Petroglyphs]. They cast and resolve [Crowd's Favor], targeting Grizzly Bears. Amia then casts [Archetype of Courage]. After it resolves, what are the power and toughness of Grizzly Bears?
answer:
Grizzly Bears is 5/4.

Why: Grizzly Bears' printed power/toughness is 2/2. Crowd's Favor gave it +1/+0 and granted it first strike until end of turn. While Grizzly Bears actually had the granted first strike ability, Muraganda Petroglyphs ("Creatures with no abilities get +2/+2") did not apply, because a granted ability is a real ability — rule 113.12 explicitly uses Muraganda Petroglyphs and an "enchanted creature has flying" Aura as the example. So at that point Grizzly Bears was 3/2.

When Amia's Archetype of Courage resolves, its second ability says creatures Amia's opponents control "lose first strike and can't have or gain first strike." Nathanael is an opponent of Amia, so Grizzly Bears loses the first strike granted by Crowd's Favor. Grizzly Bears now has no abilities again, so Muraganda Petroglyphs' +2/+2 starts applying — rule 613.5 confirms these layer recalculations are continual, automatic, and instantaneous, so nothing needs to "re-trigger."

Losing first strike does not undo the +1/+0; that part of Crowd's Favor's effect is independent and still applies in layer 7c. Both Crowd's Favor's +1/+0 and Muraganda Petroglyphs' +2/+2 are layer 7c modifications (613.4c), applied in timestamp order (613.7), and since they're simple additive modifiers the order doesn't change the total: 2/2 + 1/+0 + 2/+2 = 5/4.

This result doesn't depend on the number of players: Archetype of Courage's ability affects creatures controlled by any of its controller's opponents, so in a multiplayer game every opponent's creatures (including Nathanael's Grizzly Bears) lose first strike the same way.

question: Albert controls [Life and Limb], [Blood Moon], and [Murmuring Bosk], that entered the battlefield in that order. Is Murmuring Bosk a creature?
answer:
No — Murmuring Bosk is not a creature; it's just a land (a Mountain) as long as Blood Moon is on the battlefield.

Why:

1. Life and Limb only affects Forests and Saprolings: "All Forests and all Saprolings are 1/1 green Saproling creatures and Forest lands in addition to their other types." So Murmuring Bosk would need the land subtype Forest for Life and Limb to touch it.
2. Murmuring Bosk is a nonbasic land. Its type line is "Land — Forest," but it lacks the "basic" supertype, and any land without that supertype is nonbasic even though it has a basic land type [305.8] [205.4c] [Nonbasic Land] [Murmuring Bosk ruling #0].
3. Blood Moon says "Nonbasic lands are Mountains." That's an effect that sets the object's land subtype rather than granting an ability [113.12], and it applies continuously without using the stack [405.6b]. Because Murmuring Bosk is nonbasic, Blood Moon replaces its land subtype with Mountain — it is no longer a Forest.
4. With Murmuring Bosk being a Mountain and not a Forest (and not a Saproling), Life and Limb has nothing to apply to, so Murmuring Bosk is not a 1/1 green Saproling creature. Note that Life and Limb also grants no ability to tap for {G} on its own; Murmuring Bosk's mana abilities are likewise rewritten by Blood Moon into the Mountain ability "{T}: Add {R}."

Timing/order assumption: you gave the order Life and Limb, then Blood Moon, then Murmuring Bosk. That ordering doesn't change the outcome here — Blood Moon's effect determines whether Murmuring Bosk is a Forest at all, so Life and Limb's condition is simply never met. Be aware that the detailed layer/dependency and timestamp rules (rule 613) were not included in the context I was given; I'm relying on the fact that Blood Moon's type-setting effect determines Murmuring Bosk's land subtype, which is what Life and Limb keys on.

Side note on Life and Limb's rulings: they confirm that when Life and Limb does apply, Forests are land creatures that trigger both creature-enters and land-enters abilities, and each subtype stays correlated to its own card type — Forest is a land type, Saproling is a creature type [Life and Limb ruling #3] [205.3c]. None of that helps Murmuring Bosk while Blood Moon is out.

Multiplayer: this answer is about characteristics of permanents only, so it's identical whether the game has two players or more — no defending-player or turn-order question arises. If Blood Moon leaves the battlefield, Murmuring Bosk reverts to being a Forest and Life and Limb immediately makes it a 1/1 green Saproling creature Forest land.

question: Angelica controls a [Blood Moon], a [Life and Limb], and a [Sheltered Thicket], that entered the battlefield in that order. Is the Sheltered Thicket a creature?
answer:
No — Angelica's Sheltered Thicket is not a creature; it's just a land (a Mountain).

Why: Blood Moon says "Nonbasic lands are Mountains." That's a type-changing effect applied in layer 4, and it sets the land subtype of every nonbasic land to Mountain, so Sheltered Thicket's printed subtypes Mountain Forest are replaced by Mountain alone — it is no longer a Forest [613.6].

Life and Limb says "All Forests and all Saprolings are 1/1 green Saproling creatures and Forest lands in addition to their other types." It only applies to Forests and Saprolings. Since Blood Moon has the earlier timestamp and its subtype-setting effect is applied first in layer 4, Sheltered Thicket is not a Forest when Life and Limb checks, and it is not a Saproling either, so Life and Limb never applies to it. Nothing makes it a creature, and (per [208.3a]) a noncreature permanent has no power or toughness, so it has none.

Note that Forest is a land type, not a creature type, which is exactly the subtype Blood Moon is overwriting here [205.3c] [Life and Limb ruling #3]. Also, Sheltered Thicket's own "This land enters tapped" applied as it entered [603.6d]; that's independent of the creature question.

One caveat on order: if instead Life and Limb had a later timestamp than Blood Moon, it still wouldn't matter — Life and Limb grants the Forest land type only to things that are already Forests or Saprolings, and Blood Moon continuously keeps Sheltered Thicket's land type as Mountain only, so there is no feedback loop making it a Forest.

This analysis doesn't depend on the number of players; it's the same in a two-player or multiplayer game.

question: Alfred controls a [Blood Moon], a [Life and Limb], and a 1/1 Green Saproling Creature token, that entered the battlefield in that order. What is the Saproling?
answer:
The Saproling ends up as a 1/1 green Saproling Mountain — a creature and a land — with the intrinsic ability "{T}: Add {R}" and no longer a Forest.

How it gets there:

1. The token was created as a 1/1 green Saproling creature token with no other characteristics [111.3], so it has no "basic" supertype and, once it becomes a land, it is a nonbasic land [Nonbasic Land], [205.4b].
2. Life and Limb says "All Forests and all Saprolings are 1/1 green Saproling creatures and Forest lands in addition to their other types." Because the token is a Saproling, Life and Limb makes it both a creature and a land, with the subtypes Saproling (creature type) and Forest (land type) [Life and Limb], [Life and Limb ruling #3]. question: Alex controls a [Life and Limb], a [Blood Moon], and a 1/1 Green Saproling Creature token, that entered the battlefield in that order. What is the Saproling?
answer:
Alex's Saproling token is a 1/1 green Saproling Mountain — a creature and a land — with the ability "{T}: Add {R}" and no {T}: Add {G}. It is not a Forest.

How that comes about, in timestamp order:

1. Life and Limb says "All Forests and all Saprolings are 1/1 green Saproling creatures and Forest lands in addition to their other types." The token is a Saproling, so Life and Limb makes it a 1/1 green creature that is also a land with the land subtype Forest [Life and Limb]. Its card types are creature and land, and its subtypes are Saproling (creature type) and Forest (land type); each subtype keeps its correlation to the right card type [Life and Limb ruling #3]. As a Saproling entering as a land creature, land-ETB triggers would have seen it [Life and Limb ruling #1].

2. Because the token is now a land, Blood Moon applies to it. A token has no "basic" supertype, so it is a nonbasic land [205.4b; Nonbasic Land; Basic]. Blood Moon has the later timestamp, so its type change is applied after Life and Limb's, which is why Forest (and "{T}: Add {G}") does not survive.

Because it's a token, no player is "playing a land" here — the land-per-turn rule for playing land cards from hand is irrelevant to it [305.1]. Also, the token has no characteristics beyond those its creating effect and these continuous effects give it [111.3].

question: Aubriella controls a [Life and Limb], a [Blood Moon], a [Sapseep Forest], and a 1/1 Green Saproling Creature token, that entered the battlefield in that order. What do the Sapseep Forest and Saproling look like?
answer:
Both end up as essentially the same thing: a 1/1 green Saproling Mountain land creature with "{T}: Add {R}" and no other abilities.

How we get there (layer 4, type-changing effects, applied in timestamp order — Life and Limb entered first, and Blood Moon also depends on Life and Limb since Life and Limb is what makes the Saproling token a land):

1. Life and Limb applies first: "All Forests and all Saprolings are 1/1 green Saproling creatures and Forest lands in addition to their other types." Sapseep Forest (a Land — Forest) becomes a 1/1 green Saproling land creature; the Saproling token becomes a 1/1 green Saproling creature that is also a Forest land. Subtypes stay correlated to their card types — Forest is the land type, Saproling the creature type ([Life and Limb ruling #3], [205.3c]).
2. Blood Moon then applies: "Nonbasic lands are Mountains." Neither Sapseep Forest nor the Saproling token has the "basic" supertype, so both are nonbasic lands ([205.4c]) — and the token only qualifies at all because Life and Limb made it a land. Each loses its other land types and its own land abilities and gains the land type Mountain plus "{T}: Add {R}" ([Blood Moon ruling #2]). So Forest is stripped off both, along with Sapseep Forest's "{G}, {T}: You gain 1 life" ability and the intrinsic "{T}: Add {G}" from being a Forest ([305.6], [Life and Limb ruling #2]).

Even though they are no longer Forests once Blood Moon is applied, Life and Limb keeps applying to the same objects in its other layers ([613.6]): the color-changing part (green, layer 5), the type-adding part it already applied (Saproling creature), and the power/toughness-setting part (1/1, layer 7b). Card text overrides nothing here — the two enchantments simply stack in layer order.

Final state of each:
- Sapseep Forest — Land Creature — Mountain Saproling, green, 1/1, "{T}: Add {R}". Because it hasn't been a creature you've controlled since your turn began, it's summoning sick and you can't pay the {T} cost of that mana ability this turn ([Life and Limb ruling #0]).
- The Saproling token — Land Creature — Mountain Saproling, green, 1/1, "{T}: Add {R}". Same summoning-sickness caveat while it's newly under your control.

This is all a one-player board state; nothing here changes between a two-player and a multiplayer game.

answer:

Cinder Glade is nonbasic, so it loses the Forest type, loses its own printed abilities (including the "enters tapped unless you control two or more basic lands" clause, which is irrelevant now anyway since it's already on the battlefield), and is only a Mountain. Life and Limb only animates Forests and Saprolings; Cinder Glade is neither once Blood Moon has applied, so Life and Limb does nothing to it.

Life and Limb's power/toughness- and color-setting parts keep applying to it in their own layers even after its land type changes ([613.5], [613.6]). The dependency/timestamp rules that formally settle that ordering (613.7–613.8) weren't included in the context I was given, so I've applied the ordering that follows from Blood Moon being able to affect anything that is a nonbasic land. If instead Blood Moon were held not to apply to the token at all, the token would keep the Forest land type and tap for {G} instead of {R}; its 1/1 green Saproling creature-land status would be the same either way. question: Alannah controls [Ore-Rich Stalactite], [Life and Limb], [March of the Machines], and [Xenograft] naming "Saproling", that entered the battlefield in that order. What is the Ore-Rich Stalactite?
answer:
Ore-Rich Stalactite ends up being a 2/2 green Artifact Land Creature with the subtypes Forest and Saproling — it keeps being an artifact, gains creature and land types, and taps for either {R} (for instants/sorceries only, from its own printed ability) or {G} (intrinsically, from being a Forest).

How it gets there (layer 4, type-changing, then layer 7b, P/T setting):

1. March of the Machines makes each noncreature artifact an artifact creature. Ore-Rich Stalactite is a noncreature artifact, so it becomes an artifact creature.
2. Xenograft (naming Saproling) makes each creature Alannah controls a Saproling in addition to its other types. This only works because March of the Machines already made Ore-Rich Stalactite a creature, so March of the Machines is applied first.
3. Life and Limb makes all Forests and all Saprolings 1/1 green Saproling creatures and Forest lands in addition to their other types. Ore-Rich Stalactite is now a Saproling (thanks to Xenograft), so Life and Limb catches it too. Xenograft is applied before Life and Limb because Xenograft changes what Life and Limb applies to (a dependency), even though Life and Limb entered earlier.

Result of layer 4: Ore-Rich Stalactite is an Artifact Land Creature — Saproling Forest. Being a land with the basic land type Forest, it gains the intrinsic ability "{T}: Add {G}" [305.6], on top of its own "{T}: Add {R}. Spend this mana only to cast an instant or sorcery spell" and its craft ability. Note it is not a Mountain and does not gain "{T}: Add {R}" from a land type; the {R} comes only from its own printed ability and is restricted to instants and sorceries.

Color (layer 5): Life and Limb makes it green.

Power/toughness (layer 7b): two effects set P/T — March of the Machines sets it to its mana value (2/2) and Life and Limb sets it to 1/1. Per [613.6] each part of an effect applies in its own layer to the same set of objects, and within layer 7b these two independent setting effects are ordered by timestamp. Life and Limb entered first, March of the Machines second, so March of the Machines is applied last and wins: Ore-Rich Stalactite is 2/2 (its mana value is 2). The dependency that reordered them in layer 4 doesn't apply in layer 7b, because applying one of these P/T settings doesn't change what the other does.

Practical notes: as a creature it's subject to summoning sickness unless Alannah has controlled it continuously since her turn began, so it can't use its {T} abilities before then. It's now an artifact land, subject to the rules for both card types [Artifact Land], and Life and Limb also means anything that destroys Forests or Saprolings hits it.

Assumption on ordering: I've used the entry order you gave (Ore-Rich Stalactite, Life and Limb, March of the Machines, Xenograft) for timestamps. If March of the Machines had entered before Life and Limb instead, Life and Limb would be the later timestamp in layer 7b and Ore-Rich Stalactite would be 1/1 instead of 2/2; all its types and colors would be unchanged.

Player count doesn't matter here — none of these effects reference opponents, so the answer is the same in a two-player game or a multiplayer game.

question: Ainsley controls [Furycalm Snarl], [Humility], [Magus of the Moon], and [Crosis's Catacombs] that entered the battlefield in that order. What are the characteristics of the Furycalm Snarl and Crosis's Catacombs?

Neither land is changed at all: Magus of the Moon's ability is gone.

Humility says "All creatures lose all abilities and have base power and toughness 1/1." Magus of the Moon is a creature (Human Wizard), so Humility strips its ability "Nonbasic lands are Mountains" and makes it a 1/1. Because Humility also has the earlier timestamp here (it entered before Magus of the Moon), there's no dependency/timestamp trick that saves the ability — ability-removal is applied before the land-type-changing effect could exist, so nothing ever turns nonbasic lands into Mountains (characteristics are determined by applying continuous effects in layers, rule 613.1).

Result:

If you don't, this land enters tapped" and "{T}: Add {R} or {W}." Note {R} and {W} are single-color mana, not generic.
- Crosis's Catacombs: a colorless Land — Lair named Crosis's Catacombs with "When this land enters, sacrifice it unless you return a non-Lair land you control to its owner's hand" (that trigger already resolved on entry) and "{T}: Add {U}, {B}, or {R}."

question: Aiden controls [Volrath's Shapeshifter] and [Yixlid Jailer]. The top card of their graveyard is [Mistform Skyreaver]. Does Volrath's Shapeshifter have flying?
answer:
No — Volrath's Shapeshifter does not have flying in this situation.

Why: Yixlid Jailer says "Cards in graveyards lose all abilities," so the Mistform Skyreaver card sitting on top of Aiden's graveyard has no abilities at all while it's there — no flying and no "{1}: This creature becomes the creature type of your choice until end of turn." Volrath's Shapeshifter's static ability gives it "the full text of that card," and per [612.6] "full text" changes not only the text box and type line but also the name, mana cost, color indicator, power, and toughness. So Volrath's Shapeshifter still takes on Mistform Skyreaver's name, {5}{U}{U} mana cost (five generic plus two blue), color, creature type Illusion, and 6/6 power/toughness — but since the ability-granting text is what Yixlid Jailer has stripped from the graveyard card, there is no flying ability for Volrath's Shapeshifter to copy.

Volrath's Shapeshifter also keeps its own granted ability "{2}: Discard a card" ([Volrath's Shapeshifter ruling #1]), so the result is a 6/6 blue Illusion named Mistform Skyreaver with only "{2}: Discard a card" and no evasion. Flying is the evasion keyword that means a creature can't be blocked except by creatures with flying and/or reach ([702.9a], [702.9b]); without it, any creature can block this permanent.

Note also that artwork or flavor is irrelevant — a creature only has flying if its rules text grants it ([203.1]).

This interaction doesn't depend on the number of players; it works the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table, since Yixlid Jailer affects cards in all graveyards.

question: Nickolas controls [Dryad Arbor]. Aniya casts [Overwhelming Splendor], enchanting Nickolas. After it resolves, can Nickolas tap the Dryad Arbor for {G}?
answer:
No. Nickolas can't get {G} from Dryad Arbor while Overwhelming Splendor enchants him.

Why: Dryad Arbor is a Land Creature — Forest Dryad, and its "{T}: Add {G}" is an intrinsic ability it has because it has the basic land type Forest [305.6]. Overwhelming Splendor says "Creatures enchanted player controls lose all abilities and have base power and toughness 1/1." Dryad Arbor is a creature Nickolas controls, so it loses all of its abilities — including the intrinsic Forest mana ability. With no mana ability at all, there is nothing to activate that would add {G}; tapping it for mana means activating a mana ability that includes {T} in its cost [106.12a/106.12b], and that ability no longer exists.

Note the second sentence of Overwhelming Splendor ("Enchanted player can't activate abilities that aren't mana abilities or loyalty abilities") doesn't help here — it would have permitted mana abilities, but the first sentence already stripped Dryad Arbor's only one. Also note that an ability granted to Dryad Arbor *after* Overwhelming Splendor became attached would not be lost [Overwhelming Splendor ruling #5], so, for example, a later effect granting it a mana ability could give Nickolas green mana again. And if Dryad Arbor stops being a creature (or Overwhelming Splendor leaves), it gets its Forest ability back.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Overwhelming Splendor is already on the battlefield attached to Nickolas, as stated. If Nickolas taps Dryad Arbor for {G} while Overwhelming Splendor is still a spell on the stack, that mana ability resolves normally and he does get {G} — the mana stays in his pool even after Overwhelming Splendor resolves.

question: Nico controls [Yixlid Jailer]. Achilles uses [Past in Flames] to give [Deadly Complication] in their graveyard Flashback. Is Achilles able to cast Deadly Complication from their graveyard to destroy Yixlid Jailer?
answer:
No — Achilles can't cast Deadly Complication from the graveyard while Nico's Yixlid Jailer is on the battlefield.

Why: Yixlid Jailer says "Cards in graveyards lose all abilities." Flashback is a static ability that functions while the card is in a player's graveyard, and it's what gives permission to cast the card from there ([702.34a]). Past in Flames grants that flashback ability to Deadly Complication while Deadly Complication sits in Achilles's graveyard, but Yixlid Jailer strips all abilities from cards in graveyards — including granted ones — so Deadly Complication has no flashback ability there and there is nothing permitting Achilles to cast it. This is exactly the situation described in [Yixlid Jailer ruling #0]: when a card's own ability (such as flashback) is what lets you cast it from your graveyard, Yixlid Jailer stops that ability. Contrast that with an outside effect that itself says "you may cast target card from your graveyard" — that permission comes from the other spell, not from the card in the graveyard, so Yixlid Jailer wouldn't stop it (and once the card is moved to the stack it's no longer in the graveyard, so its alternative/additional costs can apply).

So Achilles's only route is to destroy or remove Yixlid Jailer first; if Yixlid Jailer leaves the battlefield while it's still the same turn, Deadly Complication regains the flashback Past in Flames granted (that grant lasts until end of turn) and Achilles could then cast it, paying its flashback cost equal to its mana cost, {1}{B}{R}, and choosing the "Destroy target creature" mode. Timing note: as a sorcery cast via flashback it can only be cast when a sorcery could normally be cast ([Past in Flames ruling #10]), and after resolving it will be exiled ([Past in Flames ruling #9]).

One more point: targeting Yixlid Jailer, a permanent an opponent controls, means Achilles commits a crime ([700.13]) — relevant only if some card cares. Nothing here depends on the number of players; the rules quoted apply the same in two-player and multiplayer games (in multiplayer, Yixlid Jailer's effect applies to every graveyard regardless of who controls it).

question: Aspen controls [Watchwolf] enchanted by [Lignify], [Figure of Destiny] that's had its third ability activated, and [Swab Goblin]. They casts [Pack's Favor] targeting Swab Goblin. After that resolves, they casts [Mirrorweave] targeting Figure of Destiny. What are the characteristics of Swab Goblin and Watchwolf?
answer:
Direct answer: After Mirrorweave resolves, Swab Goblin is a red 4/4 creature named Figure of Destiny — Creature — Kithkin, mana cost {R/W}... actually its mana cost becomes {R/W} (so it's red-and-white, not red), and it has Figure of Destiny's three activated abilities; it's 1/1 base plus Pack's Favor's +3/+3 = 4/4. Watchwolf is a red-and-white 0/4 creature named Figure of Destiny, Creature — Treefolk, mana cost {R/W}, with no abilities.

Why:

1) Mirrorweave copies only the *copiable values* of Figure of Destiny — the values from its printed text: name Figure of Destiny, mana cost {R/W} (hence red and white), Creature — Kithkin, 1/1, and its three activated abilities [707.2a]. The fact that Figure of Destiny's second ability was activated (making it a 4/4 Kithkin Spirit Warrior) is a non-copiable type-changing/P-T-setting effect, so it is NOT copied [707.2a]. Note the question says the "third ability" was activated; either way, resolved activations of Figure of Destiny's abilities are ignored for copying, so the copies start as 1/1 Kithkin.

2) Copy effects apply in layer 1a, before any other effect [613.1a, 613.2a, 613.2c]. So each creature first becomes printed Figure of Destiny, then other effects are layered on top.

3) Swab Goblin: copy in layer 1 gives 1/1 Kithkin named Figure of Destiny with the three {R/W} abilities. Pack's Favor's +3/+3 is a later power/toughness-modifying effect, and it stays on Swab Goblin's new object → 4/4. Its controller can still activate the Figure of Destiny abilities it now has (they'd set base 2/2, etc., and the +3/+3 would still add on top).

4) Watchwolf: copy in layer 1 makes it Figure of Destiny (1/1 Kithkin, {R/W}, three abilities). Lignify is still attached and still applies afterward: enchanted creature is a Treefolk with base power and toughness 0/4 and loses all abilities. So the creature types become Treefolk (overwriting Kithkin), all abilities — including the three copied Figure of Destiny abilities — are removed, and base P/T is set to 0/4. Lignify overrides characteristic-defining P/T and type abilities as well [Lignify ruling #5]. Name, mana cost, and color come from the copy: Figure of Destiny, {R/W}, red and white [707.2a, 707.3]. Result: red-and-white 0/4 Creature — Treefolk named Figure of Destiny, no abilities.

5) Figure of Destiny itself is unchanged — Mirrorweave affects "each other creature."

Timing note: I'm assuming Pack's Favor fully resolved before Mirrorweave was cast, as stated. If instead Pack's Favor were still on the stack and resolved after Mirrorweave, the +3/+3 would simply apply later and Swab Goblin's result would be the same 4/4, since layers, not resolution order, determine the outcome [613.1a, 613.7].

Only Aspen's own creatures are discussed here; Mirrorweave hits every other creature on the battlefield, so with more than two players it would also copy Figure of Destiny onto every other player's creatures the same way.

question: Allison controls [Dralnu's Crusade] and [Leopard-Spotted Jiao]. Allison then casts [Conspiracy] naming "Goblin". What are the creature types of Leopard-Spotted Jiao and does it get +1/+1?
answer:
Direct answer: Leopard‑Spotted Jiao stops being a Beast and is a Goblin (very likely Goblin Zombie), it becomes black, and yes — it gets +1/+1, so it's a 4/2.

Why:

1. Conspiracy says "Creatures you control are the chosen type," and its ruling [Conspiracy ruling #4] states affected creatures lose all of their other creature types. So Leopard‑Spotted Jiao loses Beast and is simply a Goblin. Beast and Goblin are both creature types (subtypes shared by creatures and kindreds) [302.3] [205.3m] [205.3b].

2. Because Leopard‑Spotted Jiao is now a Goblin, Dralnu's Crusade applies to it: "All Goblins get +1/+1" and "All Goblins are black and are Zombies in addition to their other creature types." Its power/toughness change is applied after type‑changing effects are taken into account, so Leopard‑Spotted Jiao is 4/2 and is black (black only, not red‑and‑black) [Dralnu's Crusade ruling #0].

3. On the Zombie part I have to be candid: the rules excerpts provided here don't include the layer/timestamp‑and‑dependency rules that decide the interaction of two simultaneous type‑changing effects (Conspiracy setting the type to Goblin only, Dralnu's Crusade adding Zombie to Goblins). Under normal MTG layer handling Dralnu's Crusade's type addition is applied after Conspiracy's, giving Goblin Zombie; but the provided context doesn't contain that rule, so treat "Goblin Zombie" as the expected result rather than something I can cite here. What is unambiguous from the provided material is: not a Beast, is a Goblin, is black, and gets +1/+1.

Timing note: I'm assuming Conspiracy has already resolved and is on the battlefield. While Conspiracy is still on the stack, nothing has changed yet — Leopard‑Spotted Jiao is still a 3/1 red Beast with no bonus.

Player count doesn't matter here: both Dralnu's Crusade and Conspiracy affect only Allison's own creatures (Conspiracy) or all Goblins (Dralnu's Crusade), and the context contains no multiplayer‑specific rules bearing on this.

question: Alaina has seven cards in their hand and controls [Recycle]. They cast [Trusted Advisor]. After that resolves, what is Alaina's maximum hand size?
answer:
Alaina's maximum hand size is four.

Recycle says "Your maximum hand size is two," and Trusted Advisor says "Your maximum hand size is increased by two." When multiple effects modify maximum hand size, they're applied in timestamp order (Recycle ruling #2, Trusted Advisor ruling #0). Since Recycle was already on the battlefield when Trusted Advisor entered, Recycle first sets the value to 2, then the later-timestamped Trusted Advisor adds 2, for a maximum hand size of four. (If the order were reversed — Trusted Advisor first, then Recycle — the setting effect would apply last and the maximum hand size would be two.)

Alaina keeps all seven cards for now: maximum hand size only matters during the cleanup step, when the active player discards down to their maximum hand size as a turn-based action that doesn't use the stack ([402.2], [514.1], [703.4n], Recycle ruling #1). So on Alaina's next cleanup step, if they still have seven cards and a maximum hand size of four, they discard three.

This works the same regardless of how many players are at the table; maximum hand size is a per-player value.

answer_gold: Four. Recycle sets the maximum hand size to two, and Trusted Advisor then modifies that maximum hand size by adding two to it.

question: Alisson controls [Quickening Licid], [March of the Machines], and [Mycosynth Lattice] that entered the battlefield in that order. They activate Quickening Licid's ability targeting itself. What happens?
answer:
Quickening Licid ends up in Alisson's graveyard. Because Mycosynth Lattice makes every permanent an artifact and March of the Machines makes each noncreature artifact into an artifact creature, the Aura that Quickening Licid becomes is still a creature — and an Aura that's also a creature can't enchant anything. It's unattached the next time state-based actions are checked, and is then immediately put into its owner's graveyard as a second state-based action [Mycosynth Lattice ruling #3].

Details:
- Activating Quickening Licid's {1}{W}, {T} ability makes it lose that ability and become an Aura enchantment with enchant creature, attached to the target creature (here, itself, which is a legal creature target at activation).
- Mycosynth Lattice: "All permanents are artifacts in addition to their other types." March of the Machines: "Each noncreature artifact is an artifact creature with power and toughness each equal to its mana value." Since Quickening Licid's own effect doesn't stop it from being a creature via these effects, the resulting object is an artifact creature Aura (2/2, since Quickening Licid's mana value is 2). Type/ability-setting effects here are applied in the layer system in timestamp order [613.6][613.7], and March of the Machines' animation of the now-noncreature artifact applies to it.
- An Aura that is also a creature can't legally be attached, so the state-based actions unattach it and then put it into the graveyard [Mycosynth Lattice ruling #3].
- Timing note: Quickening Licid's "You may pay {W} to end this effect" would return it to being an ordinary creature, but state-based actions are checked before any player gets priority again, so Alisson realistically can't save it after the ability resolves; if the game state let them pay {W} while the effect was still being applied, Quickening Licid would simply stay a 1/1 creature with its abilities (compare [Quickening Licid ruling #1], where paying {W} makes it stop being an enchantment).

This outcome doesn't depend on the number of players, since only Alisson's own permanents are involved.

The “becomes the color of your choice” part is applied in layer 5, and then the “gets +1/+1” part is applied in layer 7c. Act of Treason has an effect that reads “Gain control of target creature until end of turn. Untap that creature. The “gain control” part is applied in layer 2, and then the “it gains haste” part is applied in layer 6. An effect that reads “All noncreature artifacts become 2/2 artifact creatures until end of turn” is both a type-changing effect and a power- and toughness-setting effect. The type-changing effect is applied to all noncreature artifacts in layer 4 and the power- and toughness-setting effect is applied to those same permanents in layer 7b, even though those permanents aren’t noncreature artifacts by then. question: Aya controls a [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave] with 3 +1/+1 counters on it. Nico casts [Duplicant] and has it exile Skullbriar, the Walking Grave. What are Duplicant's power and toughness after the imprint ability resolves?
answer:
Duplicant becomes 4/4.

Why: Skullbriar, the Walking Grave is printed 1/1, and its own text says "Counters remain on Skullbriar as it moves to any zone other than a player's hand or library." Exile is not hand or library, so all three +1/+1 counters stay on the card in the exile zone. A +1/+1 counter on a creature card in a zone other than the battlefield still adds to that card's power and toughness [122.1a], and Skullbriar's rulings confirm this explicitly (a Skullbriar in the command zone with one +1/+1 counter is 2/2) [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #2]. So the exiled Skullbriar, the Walking Grave card is 4/4 in exile.

Duplicant's imprint-linked static ability says it "has the power, toughness, and creature types of the last creature card exiled with it," so Duplicant takes 4/4 rather than its printed 2/4, and it remains a Shapeshifter. Duplicant's rulings note its base power and toughness become the imprinted card's, and that they are constantly updated if the exiled card's power/toughness change [Duplicant ruling #0][Duplicant ruling #3] — so if a counter were somehow removed or added in exile, Duplicant would update.

One nuance worth naming: Duplicant ruling #2 says abilities that define a * apply in exile but abilities that add or subtract power/toughness do not. That exclusion is about abilities (like Death's Shadow's), not about counters physically on the exiled card; the counters here are objects' modifiers under 122.1a, and Skullbriar's own printed text is what keeps them there, overriding the normal expectation that counters vanish on a zone change.

Anything else that then modifies Duplicant on the battlefield (counters on Duplicant, pumps, etc.) applies on top of 4/4 in layer 7 [613.1g][613.4a]. Player count doesn't matter here — the answer is the same whether it's Aya and Nico heads-up or a larger multiplayer table, since only the targeting of one creature is involved.

question: Abel attacks with [Pristine Angel]. While it's tapped, Nico activates [Cephalid Snitch]'s ability targeting Pristine Angel. After that resolves, Abel casts a spell and untaps Pristine Angel. Can Nico now target the Pristine Angel with [Murder]?
answer:
Yes — Nico can target Pristine Angel with Murder.

Why: Cephalid Snitch's ability said "Target creature loses protection from black until end of turn," and that effect lasts for the rest of the turn regardless of whether Pristine Angel is tapped or untapped. Pristine Angel's own ability ("As long as this creature is untapped, it has protection from artifacts and from each color") starts applying again when Abel untaps it, but the Cephalid Snitch effect has the later timestamp and continues to strip protection from black specifically for the duration of the turn; continuous effects like these are applied in timestamp order (rule 613.11). So on untapping, Pristine Angel has protection from artifacts and from white, blue, red, and green — but not from black. Murder is a black instant, so it's a legal target, and it will still be a legal target on resolution and destroy Pristine Angel (608.2b).

Two side notes:
- Note that Cephalid Snitch's ability only had to be legal when activated; because it was activated while Pristine Angel was tapped (no protection at all), targeting was fine.
- Nico targeting Pristine Angel, a permanent an opponent controls, is committing a crime (700.13, Crime), which matters only if some card of Nico's cares about crimes.
- Untapping Pristine Angel does not remove it from combat (506.4b), so it remains an attacking creature until Murder destroys it.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Cephalid Snitch's ability fully resolved while Pristine Angel was still tapped, as stated. If instead Pristine Angel had already untapped before that ability resolved, the ability would have had an illegal target (protection from black would have made it an illegal target) and would have been removed from the stack without effect (608.2b), and Murder could not then target Pristine Angel.

This analysis is the same whether the game has two players or more; nothing here depends on the number of opponents.

question: Alijah controls [Badlands] and [Conversion]. Alijah then casts [Magus of the Moon]. After that resolves, what color(s) of mana can Badlands tap for?
answer:
Badlands can tap only for {R} (red mana).

Why: Magus of the Moon's text "Nonbasic lands are Mountains" resolved most recently, so it applies last among the type-setting effects. Badlands is a nonbasic land, so its subtypes are set to just Mountain; per [Magus of the Moon ruling #4] and [305.7], it loses its other land types (Swamp) and the abilities from them, and gains "{T}: Add {R}" — the intrinsic Mountain mana ability from [305.6] and [Mountain]. Normally Badlands would have both of its basic land types' mana abilities ([Badlands ruling #3]), i.e. {T}: Add {B} or {R}, but a subtype-setting effect wipes the old types ([Badlands ruling #1]).

Conversion ("All Mountains are Plains") applies earlier in timestamp order, when Badlands was still a Swamp Mountain — at that point it would have been a Swamp Plains, tapping for {B} or {W}. But Magus of the Moon then re-sets the subtype to Mountain, and because Conversion's older effect has already been applied it doesn't get re-applied to the newly created Mountain. So the end state is a Mountain tapping for {R}.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Conversion was already on the battlefield before Magus of the Moon resolved, as stated. If instead Conversion entered the battlefield after Magus of the Moon, Conversion would have the later timestamp and would turn Badlands (now a Mountain) into a Plains, so it would tap for {W} instead. Note Conversion is a continuous effect, so there's no window to tap for the old color in between ([Conversion ruling #0]).

This analysis doesn't depend on player count — it's the same in a two-player or multiplayer game, since both effects affect all applicable lands regardless of controller.

question: Adriel controls [Wandering Ones] equipped with [Fleetfeather Sandals]. On Nico's turn, they enchant it with [Tightening Coils]. On Adriel's next turn, they activate Fleetfeather Sandals's equip ability, targeting Wandering Ones. After that resolves, does it have flying?
answer:
Yes — after the equip ability resolves, Wandering Ones has flying.

Why: Both effects are ability-adding/removing effects applied in layer 6, so they're ordered by timestamp, and the later one wins ([613.1f], [613.9]). Initially Fleetfeather Sandals' "Equipped creature has flying and haste" had the earlier timestamp, and Tightening Coils' "loses flying" came later, so Wandering Ones lost flying. But an Equipment receives a new timestamp each time it becomes attached to an object — including when it's re-attached to the same creature ([613.7e], [613.7a]). So activating Fleetfeather Sandals' equip ability ({2}, sorcery-speed only) targeting Wandering Ones and re-attaching it gives Fleetfeather Sandals — and the continuous effect from its static ability — a timestamp later than Tightening Coils. Applying layer 6 in timestamp order, "loses flying" applies first, then "has flying and haste," so Wandering Ones ends up with flying (and haste). This matches Tightening Coils' own ruling that an effect giving the enchanted creature flying after Tightening Coils became attached lets the creature have flying ([Tightening Coils ruling #0]).

Note Tightening Coils' -6/-0 still applies (it's a power/toughness effect in a different layer), so Wandering Ones is a -5/1 flier — effectively 0/1 for damage purposes. Nothing here depends on the number of players; the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table, since only Adriel's own permanent timestamps matter.

question: Ari controls [Bludgeon Brawl] and [Soldevi Digger]. They cast [Titania's Song]. Once it resolves, what are the characteristics of Soldevi Digger?
answer:
Soldevi Digger ends up as a colorless 2/2 artifact creature named Soldevi Digger with mana cost {2} (mana value 2) and no abilities — it is *not* an Equipment and does not have equip {2} or "Equipped creature gets +2/+0" from Bludgeon Brawl.

Why: Bludgeon Brawl only applies to "each noncreature, non-Equipment artifact," and Titania's Song only applies to "each noncreature artifact." Both are continuous effects that would apply in the same layers (type/subtype changes in layer 4, ability changes in layer 6, and Titania's Song's power/toughness setting in layer 7b) [613.1a, 613.2c, 613.6]. Normally same-layer effects are ordered by timestamp [613.7], but dependency overrides timestamps [613.8]. Titania's Song turning Soldevi Digger into an artifact creature changes whether Bludgeon Brawl applies to it at all, so Bludgeon Brawl is dependent on Titania's Song and Titania's Song is applied first. After that, Soldevi Digger is a creature, so Bludgeon Brawl simply doesn't apply to it: no Equipment subtype, no granted abilities.

So after Titania's Song resolves, Soldevi Digger loses its "{2}: Put the top card of your graveyard on the bottom of your library" ability and becomes an artifact creature with power and toughness each equal to its mana value, which is 2 (its mana cost {2} — two generic mana — is unchanged, and it stays colorless since its mana cost has no colored symbols) [105.2, 109.3].

Timing note: I'm assuming Bludgeon Brawl was already on the battlefield when Titania's Song resolved, as stated. The dependency analysis gives the same result regardless of which enchantment arrived first, because dependency, not timestamp, decides the order here [613.8].

Nothing here depends on the number of players; the answer is the same in a two-player or multiplayer game. Also note that if Titania's Song later leaves the battlefield, its own text says the effect continues until end of turn, so Soldevi Digger stays a 2/2 ability-less artifact creature (and still not an Equipment) for the rest of that turn.

question: Ariah controls [Wayward Angel] and has 7 cards in their graveyard. Nickolas casts [Turn to Frog], targeting Wayward Angel. What are Wayward Angel's characteristics after Turn to Frog resolves?
answer:
After Turn to Frog resolves, Wayward Angel is a 1/1 blue Frog creature with no abilities. It keeps its name (Wayward Angel) and its mana cost {4}{W}{W}, but it is no longer white or black, is no longer an Angel Horror, and has no flying, vigilance, trample, or the threshold sacrifice trigger.

Why, layer by layer (613.1g, 613.4a/613.4b, 613.7):
- Color (layer 5): Wayward Angel's threshold ability would make it black (and per Wayward Angel ruling #0 it would be black only, not white and black), but Turn to Frog's color-setting effect has the later timestamp, so blue wins.
- Types: Turn to Frog makes it a Frog, replacing Angel Horror.
- Abilities (layer 6): Turn to Frog says the creature "loses all abilities." With the later timestamp, it strips flying, vigilance, and the threshold ability itself, so the threshold-granted trample and "At the beginning of your upkeep, sacrifice a creature" are gone too.
- Power/toughness (layer 7): Turn to Frog sets base power and toughness to 1/1 in layer 7b (613.4b). Because the threshold ability no longer exists, its +3/+3 modification isn't applied on top, so it stays 1/1 rather than 4/4. Per Turn to Frog ruling #0, Turn to Frog also overwrites any earlier base-P/T-setting effects, and any later P/T-setting effect would overwrite it.

One timing note: this assumes Ariah still had seven or more cards in the graveyard as Turn to Frog resolved. It doesn't matter to the outcome — either way the threshold ability is gone once Turn to Frog resolves. Also, if Wayward Angel gains an ability after Turn to Frog has resolved, it keeps that new ability (Turn to Frog ruling #3). The effect lasts until end of turn.

This analysis doesn't depend on the number of players; it's the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

question: Ariella controls a manifested [Wayward Angel] and has 7 cards in their graveyard. Nathaniel casts [Turn to Frog], targeting Wayward Angel. After that resolves, Ariella turns Wayward Angel face up. What are Wayward Angel's characteristics afterwards?
answer:
Afterwards, until end of turn, Wayward Angel is a face-up 1/1 blue Frog creature named Wayward Angel with mana cost {4}{W}{W} and no abilities.

How that comes about:

1. Manifest put Wayward Angel onto the battlefield face down, so its copiable characteristics while face down were those listed by the rules that let it be face down: a 2/2 colorless creature with no name, no card types beyond creature, no abilities, and no mana cost [708.2a] [613.2b].
2. Turn to Frog resolved on that face-down permanent: "Until end of turn, target creature loses all abilities and becomes a blue Frog with base power and toughness 1/1." Per Turn to Frog ruling #1, it loses other colors and creature types but keeps other card types/supertypes.
3. When Ariella turns Wayward Angel face up, its copiable values revert to its normal printed values — name Wayward Angel, mana cost {4}{W}{W}, Creature — Angel Horror, 4/4, flying, vigilance, and the Threshold ability — but "any effects that have been applied to the face-down permanent still apply to the face-up permanent" [708.8]. Turn to Frog is still applying.
4. Applying continuous effects in layers: Turn to Frog's ability-removal and type/color change wipe flying, vigilance, and the Threshold ability, and make it a blue Frog; its base power/toughness are set to 1/1, and no later P/T-setting effect exists [613.1] [613.1g] [Turn to Frog ruling #0]. Because the Threshold ability is removed, the +3/+3, black, trample, and the upkeep sacrifice trigger never apply, even with seven cards in Ariella's graveyard — so it is blue, not black [Wayward Angel ruling #0].

Timing note: I'm assuming Turn to Frog fully resolved before Wayward Angel was turned face up, as stated. If instead Wayward Angel were turned face up first and Turn to Frog resolved afterward, the end result for the rest of the turn would be the same 1/1 blue Frog with no abilities. Also note that manifest/turning face up doesn't retrigger any enters-the-battlefield abilities [708.8].

Nothing here depends on player count; the answer is the same at a two-player or multiplayer table.

question: Ahmad controls [Conspiracy] (naming "Ferret"), [Kormus Bell], [Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth], and a [Vastwood Zendikon] enchanting Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth that entered the battlefield in that order. Is Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth a creature? If so, what are its creature types?
answer:
Yes — Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth is a creature, and its only creature type is Ferret.

How it gets there:

1. Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth's own ability makes each land a Swamp in addition to its other land types, and that includes Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth itself while it's on the battlefield [Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth ruling #0][Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth ruling #2].
2. Kormus Bell then makes all Swamps 1/1 black creatures that are still lands, so Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth becomes a land creature — both card types at once, affected by anything affecting either [Kormus Bell ruling #0][205.1b][205.2b]. Kormus Bell grants no creature type.
3. Vastwood Zendikon makes the enchanted land a 6/4 green Elemental creature that's still a land [Vastwood Zendikon ruling #5], which would give the creature type Elemental.
4. Conspiracy makes creatures Ahmad controls the chosen type, and affected creatures lose all their other creature types [Conspiracy ruling #4]. Conspiracy explicitly can grant a creature type to animated lands and artifacts that would otherwise have none [Conspiracy ruling #1]. So the Elemental type is replaced and Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth is just a Ferret — a legal one-word creature type [205.3m].

So Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth is a legendary land creature (a 6/4 green Ferret from Vastwood Zendikon's later power/toughness- and color-setting effect over Kormus Bell's 1/1 black), still a Swamp and still legendary, since changing card types or subtypes doesn't strip supertypes [205.4b][205.3c].

Two caveats: (a) the numbered layer/timestamp rules that formally order Conspiracy's type-setting against Vastwood Zendikon's "Elemental" weren't provided here; I'm relying on Conspiracy's ruling that affected creatures lose all other creature types, which is authoritative on the outcome. (b) Nothing here depends on the number of players, so the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table — Conspiracy only affects creatures Ahmad controls and cards he owns.

question: Andre controls [Raugrin Triome] and [Prismatic Omen]. Nala casts [Blood Moon]. After it resolves, what land types does Raugrin Triome have?
answer:
Raugrin Triome ends up with the single land type Mountain (and only the ability "{T}: Add {R}").

Why: Blood Moon says "Nonbasic lands are Mountains," and per [Blood Moon ruling #2] nonbasic lands lose any other land types and abilities they had, gaining the land type Mountain and "{T}: Add {R}." Raugrin Triome is a nonbasic land — [Prismatic Omen ruling #1] confirms that granting extra basic land types does not make a land basic, and Blood Moon ruling #1 likewise notes Blood Moon doesn't change supertypes, so Raugrin Triome stays nonbasic and is affected.

Because Nala's Blood Moon resolved after Andre's Prismatic Omen was already on the battlefield, Blood Moon has the later timestamp: Prismatic Omen first makes Raugrin Triome all five basic land types (Plains, Island, Swamp, Mountain, Forest) per [Prismatic Omen ruling #0], and then Blood Moon wipes those away, leaving just Mountain. Its Island/Mountain/Plains printed types and its "{T}: Add {U}, {R}, or {W}" ability are gone too; it now taps only for {R} ([305.6], [Mountain]). Its name, its "enters tapped" ability text as printed being a static land-type-independent ability aside, and its Cycling {3} in hand are not land types and aren't the issue here.

Timing caveat: I'm assuming Prismatic Omen was already on the battlefield when Blood Moon resolved, as stated. If Andre later re-established a Prismatic Omen effect (a new Prismatic Omen entering after Blood Moon), that newer timestamp would apply last and Raugrin Triome would again have all five basic land types, tapping for any color.

Player count doesn't matter here — this works the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table, since Blood Moon affects all nonbasic lands regardless of controller.

question: Apollo controls [Realmwright] naming "Island", [Arcane Adaptation] naming "Saproling", and [Life and Limb], which entered the battlefield in that order. What are the types and subtypes of Realmwright?
answer:
Realmwright ends up as a **Land Creature — Forest Island Vedalken Wizard Saproling**, a 1/1 green permanent.

How it gets there, in layers/order:

1. Printed: Creature — Vedalken Wizard, 1/1 [205.3b].
2. Arcane Adaptation (Saproling chosen) makes creatures you control that type in addition to their other types, so Realmwright is now also a Saproling [Arcane Adaptation ruling #1].
3. Because Realmwright is now a Saproling, Life and Limb applies to it: "All Forests and all Saprolings are 1/1 green Saproling creatures and Forest lands in addition to their other types." Realmwright therefore gains the land card type and the land type Forest, keeps the creature type and its creature types, and becomes 1/1 and green [205.1b], [Life and Limb ruling #3]. Each subtype stays correlated to the proper card type — Forest is a land type, Saproling/Vedalken/Wizard are creature types [205.3c], [Life and Limb ruling #3].
4. Now that Realmwright is a land you control, its own ability applies to itself: "Lands you control are the chosen type in addition to their other types," adding the basic land type Island [205.3i], [Realmwright ruling #1].

Consequences: as a Forest and an Island it has the intrinsic abilities "{T}: Add {G}" and "{T}: Add {U}" [305.6], [Island]. Since it's also a creature, it's subject to summoning sickness, so it can't be tapped for mana or attack unless you've controlled it continuously since your most recent turn began (per Life and Limb's own reminder text). It does not lose any supertypes it might have had [205.4b].

I assumed the entry order given (Realmwright, then Arcane Adaptation, then Life and Limb); the final result is the same regardless of that order, since all three are continuous static effects that reapply constantly. Nothing here depends on player count, so the answer is identical in two-player and multiplayer games — all three effects only ever look at permanents Apollo controls (Life and Limb affects all Forests and Saprolings, including opponents', but that doesn't change Realmwright's own types).

question: Ainsley controls [Leyline of Singularity] and [Awoken Demon] equipped with [Helm of the Host]. When the trigger from Helm of the Host resolves, will the created token be legendary?
answer:
Yes — the token will be legendary, and that means Ainsley immediately has to apply the legend rule.

Why: Helm of the Host says the token "isn't legendary," and that exception is copiable [Helm of the Host ruling #3]. But Leyline of Singularity is a separate continuous effect that says "All nonland permanents are legendary," and it applies to the token once the token is on the battlefield. Adding the legendary supertype this way doesn't overwrite the token's other supertypes [Leyline of Singularity ruling #0], and gaining a supertype doesn't change its card types or subtypes [205.4b]. So Helm of the Host's exception only means the token isn't legendary from the copy effect; Leyline of Singularity makes it legendary anyway.

Consequence: any legendary permanent is subject to the legend rule [205.4d, 704.5j]. Since the token is a copy of the equipped creature, it has that creature's name (Awoken Demon, the face-up face of Ecstatic Awakener // Awoken Demon), and Ainsley also controls the original, which Leyline of Singularity likewise makes legendary. Ainsley controls two legendary permanents with the same name, so as a state-based action Ainsley chooses one to keep and the other is put into its owner's graveyard [704.5j]. The same principle Leyline of Singularity's own ruling describes for duplicate tokens applies here [Leyline of Singularity ruling #2]. If Ainsley keeps the token, it goes to the graveyard as a token and then ceases to exist as a state-based check; if Ainsley keeps the original Awoken Demon, the token dies.

Timing note: I'm assuming Leyline of Singularity is already on the battlefield when Helm of the Host's beginning-of-combat trigger resolves. If Leyline of Singularity weren't there, the token would be nonlegendary and could coexist with the original, since the legend rule needs two or more *legendary* permanents with the same name [Helm of the Host ruling #3].

This answer doesn't depend on player count — it's all about permanents Ainsley controls, so it's identical in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table.

It loses the basic land types Dryad of the Ilysian Grove had granted and loses its printed abilities "{T}: Add {C}" and "{1}, {T}: Add one mana of any color…", gaining just "{T}: Add {R}" ([Blood Moon ruling #2]). Changing its land type doesn't stop it being a green Dryad creature ([Dryad Arbor ruling #0], [Dryad Arbor ruling #2], [Dryad Arbor ruling #3], [205.3c]).

• Mountain — a basic land, unaffected by Blood Moon; Dryad of the Ilysian Grove makes it every basic land type (Plains, Island, Swamp, Mountain, Forest) with all five corresponding mana abilities ([305.6], [Dryad of the Ilysian Grove ruling #0]).

Assumption on timing: Blood Moon is cast after Dryad of the Ilysian Grove is already on the battlefield, so Blood Moon's type-setting applies last to nonbasic lands. If instead Dryad of the Ilysian Grove entered after Blood Moon, Study Hall and Dryad Arbor would be Mountains first and then gain all five basic land types and all five basic mana abilities. The provided context doesn't include the layer/timestamp rules (rule 613) themselves, so that ordering point rests on the card rulings rather than a quoted numbered rule.

All of this is independent of player count — nothing here depends on the number of opponents.

question: Angelina has seven cards in their hand, controls [Trusted Advisor], and casts [Null Profusion]. After Angelina discards at the end of the turn, how many cards should they have in their hand?
answer:
Angelina discards down to two cards. Because Null Profusion entered the battlefield after Trusted Advisor, Null Profusion has the later timestamp, so it sets Angelina's maximum hand size to two and Trusted Advisor's earlier +2 effect is already accounted for/overwritten in that order [Trusted Advisor ruling #0], [Null Profusion ruling #3].

How it works: maximum hand size is the number of cards a player must discard down to as a turn-based action at the beginning of their cleanup step [402.2], [514.1], [703.4n]. The default is seven, but effects can modify or set it; when several effects do, they're applied in timestamp order [Trusted Advisor ruling #0]. Order here: Trusted Advisor first (7 + 2 = 9), then Null Profusion sets it to two — the setting effect applied last wins, so the answer is two, not four. Had Null Profusion already been on the battlefield and Trusted Advisor entered afterward, the maximum would instead be four.

Note also that Null Profusion's "Whenever you play a card, draw a card" may add cards during the turn, but whatever Angelina's hand is when the cleanup step begins, they discard down to two, so they end with two cards. This is a rule about the affected player only, so it's the same in a two-player game or a multiplayer game.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.613.10: Some continuous effects affect players rather than objects. For example, an effect might give a player protection from red. All such effects are applied in timestamp order after the determination of objects’ characteristics. See also the rules for timestamp order and dependency (rules 613.7 and 613.8).

cited_text.402.2: Each player has a maximum hand size, which is normally seven cards. A player may have any number of cards in their hand, but as part of their cleanup step, the player must discard excess cards down to the maximum hand size.
cited_text.514.1: First, if the active player’s hand contains more cards than their maximum hand size (normally seven), they discard enough cards to reduce their hand size to that number. This turn-based action doesn’t use the stack.
cited_text.703.4n: The turn-based actions are as follows: Immediately after the cleanup step begins, if the active player’s hand contains more cards than their maximum hand size (normally seven), they discard enough cards to reduce their hand size to that number. See rule 514.1.

answer_gold: Two. Trusted Advisor adds two to the maximum hand size (making it nine), and Null Profusion then sets the maximum hand to two.

question: Nico controls [Thespian's Stage] that's currently a copy of [Temple of Triumph]. Alayna casts [Alpine Moon] and names "Temple of Triumph" as it resolves. Alayna then activates a second Thespian's Stage targeting Temple of Triumph. What does each Thespian's Stage look like?
answer:
Direct answer: Nico's Thespian's Stage (currently a copy of Temple of Triumph) is hit by Alpine Moon — it keeps the name Temple of Triumph and is still a land, but it loses all land types and all abilities (no "enters tapped," no scry trigger, no {T}: Add {R} or {W}, and not even Thespian's Stage's own abilities) and instead has only "{T}: Add one mana of any color." Alayna's own Thespian's Stage becomes a normal copy of Temple of Triumph and is unaffected by Alpine Moon, because Alpine Moon only affects lands Alayna's opponents control.

Why Nico's land is affected: Thespian's Stage's ability says it "becomes a copy of target land, except it has this ability," so its copiable values (including its name) are those of Temple of Triumph, with the Stage ability added as part of the copy process (rules 707.2, 707.9a, 707.9b, 613.2a). Alpine Moon checks the land's name, finds "Temple of Triumph," and applies. Ability-removing effects apply in a later layer than copy effects, so Alpine Moon's ability-removal wins over everything the copy gave it, including the Stage's own copy ability (613.6, 613.7). Alpine Moon does not change card types or supertypes, so it is still a land — just a typeless, ability-stripped one with the any-color mana ability (Alpine Moon ruling #1).

Alayna's second Thespian's Stage: it copies the printed/copiable values of the targeted Temple of Triumph and keeps the Stage ability. It loses Thespian's Stage's {T}: Add {C} ability (Thespian's Stage ruling #0). No enters-the-battlefield triggers or "enters tapped" effects apply, since it was already on the battlefield — so no scry (Thespian's Stage ruling #1) — and it does not untap; it's tapped from paying the activation cost (Thespian's Stage ruling #2). It can tap for {R} or {W} once untapped. Because it is Alayna's own land, Alpine Moon ("lands your opponents control") leaves it alone even though its name is Temple of Triumph.

Assumption/timing note: I'm assuming Alpine Moon's name choice was locked in as it entered (Alpine Moon says "As this enchantment enters, choose a nonbasic land card name"), and that Alayna's activation happened afterward. If Alayna's Stage had instead been targeted before Alpine Moon existed, the result is the same, since Alpine Moon's effect is continuous and checks names on an ongoing basis. Also note that if Alayna targeted Nico's Stage-as-Temple rather than a separately controlled Temple of Triumph, Alayna's Stage still becomes a plain Temple of Triumph copy: Alpine Moon's ability-loss effect is not a copiable value and isn't copied (707.2).

Multiplayer: nothing changes in structure — Alpine Moon affects every opponent of Alayna who controls a land named Temple of Triumph, and never Alayna's own lands, so at a table of three or more each opponent's copy-Temple gets stripped the same way Nico's did.

question: Allen controls [Thraben Purebloods] which is enchanted by [Kenrith's Transformation]. Thraben Purebloods then becomes enchanted by [One with the Stars]. What happens?
answer:
One with the Stars wins on card types: Thraben Purebloods stops being a creature and becomes just an enchantment.

Breaking it down:

1. Kenrith's Transformation's effect (enchanted creature loses all abilities and is a green Elk creature with base power/toughness 3/3) and One with the Stars' effect (enchanted permanent is an enchantment and loses all other card types) are two continuous effects affecting the same permanent, and neither depends on the other. They're applied in timestamp order, so the one generated later — One with the Stars — "wins" where they conflict [613.9]. Because One with the Stars became attached second, Thraben Purebloods loses the creature card type and is an enchantment only.

2. Because it's no longer a creature, it loses the subtypes tied to the card type it lost — so it isn't an Elk anymore [One with the Stars ruling #2]. It keeps any supertypes it had (Thraben Purebloods has none). It's still green from Kenrith's Transformation (color is a separate layer from card type), and Kenrith's Transformation's ability-stripping and base 3/3 still technically apply, but base power/toughness is meaningless on a noncreature permanent [613.5].

3. One with the Stars remains legally attached, since its enchant ability lets it enchant a creature or an enchantment, and Thraben Purebloods is now an enchantment [702.5c].

One caveat I can't fully ground with the rules provided: Kenrith's Transformation says "Enchant creature," and Thraben Purebloods is no longer a creature, which raises the question of whether Kenrith's Transformation becomes illegally attached. The rules excerpt here doesn't include the state-based action rule (704) that would settle that, so I'm not asserting the outcome. Note, though, that even if Kenrith's Transformation were to leave the battlefield, One with the Stars' effect keeps the permanent an enchantment and not a creature — the same principle as One with the Stars ruling #1, where the permanent stays an enchantment after a temporary creature-making effect ends.

Nothing here depends on player count, so the answer is the same in a two-player or multiplayer game.

question: Avery manifests the top card of their library with [Soul Summons]. Then, they mutate [Trumpeting Gnarr] targeting the manifested creature. What are the characteristics of the resulting creature if Avery chooses to put the manifested creature on top?
answer:
The result is a single mutated permanent that is a face-down 2/2 colorless creature with no name, no card types beyond creature, and no mana cost (the characteristics of the topmost component, the manifested card), but it has the abilities of both components — including Trumpeting Gnarr's "Whenever this creature mutates, create a 3/3 green Beast creature token" (and Trumpeting Gnarr's mutate ability).

Why: when a mutating creature spell like Trumpeting Gnarr resolves against a legal target, it doesn't enter the battlefield separately; it merges with the target creature into one object represented by both cards, and its controller chooses top or bottom [702.140c] [730.2a] [608.3d]. A mutated permanent has all abilities of each card representing it, while its other characteristics (name, mana cost, color, types, power/toughness) come from the topmost card [702.140e] [730.2a]. Since Avery put the manifested card on top, those other characteristics come from that face-down card, and a face-down manifested permanent is a 2/2 colorless creature with no name, types, or abilities of its own and no mana cost [110.5] [707.3].

Also: the merge counts as mutating, so Trumpeting Gnarr's mutate trigger goes off and Avery creates one 3/3 green Beast token [702.140d].
