question: April casts [Spontaneous Flight] targeting their [Mist Dragon]. After that resolves April then activates its 'lose flying' ability. They cast another Spontaneous Flight targeting Mist Dragon. After that resolves they then use [Hex Parasite] to remove one flying counter. Does Mist Dragon have flying?
answer:
Yes — Mist Dragon has flying.

Why: A flying counter is a keyword counter, and keyword counters grant the ability in layer 6 along with ability-adding and ability-removing effects [613.1f], [613.1]. Within layer 6, effects and counters are applied in timestamp order, with the latest applied last [613.7a], and the most recent add/remove of the same ability generally prevails [113.10c].

Sequence:
1. First Spontaneous Flight resolves: Mist Dragon gets +2/+2 until end of turn and its first flying counter (timestamp T1).
2. April activates Mist Dragon's "{0}: This creature loses flying" ability. That indefinite loss effect (T2) is later than T1, so at that moment Mist Dragon does not have flying — the loss removes all instances it applies to [113.10b].
3. Second Spontaneous Flight resolves: another +2/+2 and a second flying counter (T3), later than the loss effect at T2. Since T3 is applied after T2, Mist Dragon has flying again.
4. Hex Parasite removes one flying counter. The two counters are indistinguishable, and multiple instances of flying are redundant anyway [702.9c], so one flying counter remains — and its grant is still later than Mist Dragon's lose-flying effect. Mist Dragon still has flying.

Note that Hex Parasite could have removed both counters if April had paid a larger X (it only gets +1/+0 per counter actually removed, per [Hex Parasite ruling #0]); with both flying counters gone, the lose-flying effect would be the only layer-6 effect left and Mist Dragon would not have flying. Also, April could activate the "{0}: This creature loses flying" ability again for a new, later timestamp to strip flying without touching the counters.

This analysis doesn't depend on the number of players; nothing here involves defending-player or turn-order choices.

question: Avery casts [Vulpikeet] for its mutate cost, mutating under a 1/1 red Goblin creature token. They then cast [Rootborn Defenses], choosing to populate the merged permanent. What happens?
answer:
Populate works, and Avery gets a new token that copies the whole mutated permanent's copiable characteristics — a 1/1 red Goblin creature token with flying and "Whenever this creature mutates, put a +1/+1 counter on it" — and every creature Avery controls at that moment, including the new token, gains indestructible until end of turn.

Why:

- Casting Vulpikeet for its mutate cost made it a mutating creature spell targeting the non-Human Goblin token Avery owns [702.140a]. On resolution Vulpikeet didn't enter the battlefield; it merged with the Goblin token into a single object represented by more than one card/token, and Avery chose to put Vulpikeet on the bottom [702.140c], [608.3d], [730.1].
- Because Vulpikeet is underneath, the mutated permanent's characteristics come from the topmost component — the 1/1 red Goblin token — while it has the abilities of every component, so it's a 1/1 red Goblin token with flying and Vulpikeet's mutate trigger [702.140e]. Vulpikeet's own "Whenever this creature mutates" ability triggered on the merge and already put a +1/+1 counter on the mutated permanent, making it 2/2 [702.140d].
- Since the top component is a token, the mutated permanent is a creature token Avery controls, so it's a legal choice to populate: populate creates a token that's a copy of a creature token you control [701.36a].
- Copy effects use copiable values, and changes to characteristics caused by merging an object with a permanent are copiable [613.2a]. So the populated token copies the merged result: a 1/1 red Goblin with flying and the mutate-counter ability. It is a single new token (not itself a merged/mutated permanent), and it does not copy the +1/+1 counter, since counters aren't copiable values — the new token is 1/1 while the original mutated permanent stays 2/2.
- Rootborn Defenses populates first, then grants indestructible to creatures Avery controls as it resolves, so the newly created token does get indestructible; creatures Avery comes to control later this turn do not [Rootborn Defenses ruling #0].

Multiplayer note: nothing here depends on the number of players — the result is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table, since Vulpikeet's mutate target must be a non-Human creature with the same owner as the spell and populate only looks at Avery's own creature tokens.

question: Aimee controls [Fiend Artisan] and has four creature cards in their graveyard. Nico enchants it with [Mystic Subdual]. What is the power and toughness of Fiend Artisan?
answer:
Fiend Artisan is -1/1 (effectively 0 power when dealing damage).

Why: Fiend Artisan's printed power/toughness box is 1/1 [302.4c]. Its "This creature gets +1/+1 for each creature card in your graveyard" is an ordinary static ability that would apply in layer 7c [613.4c], not a characteristic-defining ability setting */* — Fiend Artisan's box shows real numbers, not a star [208.2a, 604.3].

Mystic Subdual makes Fiend Artisan lose all abilities, so the +1/+1-per-creature-card ability no longer exists and adds nothing, regardless of the four creature cards in Aimee's graveyard. In layer 7 you start from the printed 1/1 [613.1g], nothing sets its base P/T [613.4b], and in layer 7c the only remaining modifier is Mystic Subdual's -2/-0 [613.4c]. Result: 1-2 = -1 power, 1 toughness.

Note the Mystic Subdual ruling about */* creatures becoming 0/0 base and then -2/0 doesn't apply here, because Fiend Artisan doesn't define its power and toughness with a characteristic-defining ability [Mystic Subdual ruling #1]. Also, Fiend Artisan's bonus ability only functions on the battlefield anyway [Fiend Artisan ruling #2].

This answer is the same whether the table is two players or multiplayer — nothing here depends on player count. Timing note: it doesn't matter in what order the creature cards entered the graveyard or when Mystic Subdual was attached; while Mystic Subdual is attached, Fiend Artisan has no abilities and is -1/1. If Mystic Subdual later leaves the battlefield, the ability returns and Fiend Artisan would be 5/5 with four creature cards in the graveyard.

question: Ari controls [Xathrid Gorgon]. Neriah controls a [Hexavus] and [Stonehewer Giant]. Ari activates Xathrid Gorgon to put a petrification counter on Stonehewer Giant which Neriah removes with Hexavus. Can Neriah activate Stonehewer Giant's activated ability?
answer:
No. Neriah still can't activate Stonehewer Giant's ability. Xathrid Gorgon's ability says the targeted creature "gains defender and becomes a colorless artifact in addition to its other types. Its activated abilities can't be activated." That last part is a continuous effect created by the resolving ability, not something that depends on the petrification counter existing. The Xathrid Gorgon ruling states explicitly that the effects of Xathrid Gorgon's ability don't depend on the petrification counter — if the counter is removed, the creature remains a colorless artifact with defender, and so on [Xathrid Gorgon ruling #0]. So removing the counter with Hexavus's second ability ({1}, Remove a counter from another creature you control: Put a +1/+1 counter on Hexavus) gets Neriah a +1/+1 counter on Hexavus but does nothing to lift the restriction.

Because of that, Neriah can't even begin to activate Stonehewer Giant's {1}{W}, {T} Equipment-search ability: a player can't begin to activate an ability that's prohibited from being activated [602.5], [602.5a], and a "can't" effect beats the general permission that a player may activate an activated ability whenever they have priority [117.1b], [101.2a]. Note the cost is {1}{W} — one generic mana plus one white mana specifically — plus tapping Stonehewer Giant; the point is moot while the prohibition lasts.

Stonehewer Giant is still a creature (now also a colorless artifact) with vigilance, and it still has defender, so it can't attack either. Its static ability vigilance is unaffected by the prohibition, which only touches activated abilities [113.10], [113.12].

This answer is the same whether the game has two players or more; nothing here depends on player count.

question: Nico controls [Humility]. Avalyn controls [Maritime Guard] and wants to cast [Glowstone Recluse] mutating onto the Maritime Guard and putting it on top. What will the resulting creature's P/T be?
answer:
The merged permanent will be 1/1.

Why:

1. Mutate: because Glowstone Recluse is put on top, the merged permanent has all abilities of both cards, but its other characteristics — including printed power/toughness — come from the topmost card, Glowstone Recluse (2/3) [702.140e].
2. Layer 6 (ability-removing): Humility says "All creatures lose all abilities and have base power and toughness 1/1," so the merged permanent loses all its abilities, including Glowstone Recluse's reach and its "Whenever this creature mutates, put two +1/+1 counters on it" trigger [Humility]. Since that triggered ability doesn't exist on the battlefield while Humility is out, it never triggers and no +1/+1 counters are placed. (Compare [Humility ruling #2], which shows Humility's ability-removal in layer 6 and its P/T setting in layer 7b applying separately.)
3. Layer 7b (setting effects): Humility sets the merged permanent's base power and toughness to 1/1, overriding Glowstone Recluse's printed 2/3 [613.4b], [208.4a], [613.1].
4. Layer 7c: there are no counters or modifying effects to add, so nothing further changes [613.4c].

So the final result is a 1/1 with no abilities. Had the mutate trigger somehow resolved (for example, if Humility left the battlefield before the trigger resolved), the two +1/+1 counters would apply in layer 7c and it would be 3/3 while Humility is gone.

Timing note: I'm assuming Humility is already on the battlefield when Glowstone Recluse's mutate spell resolves. If instead Humility entered after the mutation, the two +1/+1 counters would already be on the permanent, and Humility would still set base P/T to 1/1 in layer 7b with the counters adding in layer 7c, making it 3/3 [613.4c], [613.5].

This analysis is the same regardless of the number of players at the table; nothing here depends on player count.

question: Alex controls [Magus of the Moon] and [Forgotten Monument]. Neil casts [Lizard, Connors's Curse] targeting Magus of the Moon. After Lizard, Connors's Curse has resolved, what are the characteristics of Forgotten Monument?
answer:
Forgotten Monument is still a land named Forgotten Monument, but it is now a Land — Mountain with no types or abilities of its own except "{T}: Add {R}." Losing its abilities does not stop Magus of the Moon from turning nonbasic lands into Mountains.

Why: Magus of the Moon's static ability "Nonbasic lands are Mountains" is a type-changing effect, applied in layer 4, while Lizard, Connors's Curse's ability-removing effect is applied in layer 6 [613.1d, 613.1f]. Because layer 4 is applied before layer 6 regardless of timestamps, the land-type change from Magus of the Moon continues to apply even after Magus of the Moon has lost all abilities [Magus of the Moon ruling #0].

So for Forgotten Monument:
- Card type: land. Subtype: Mountain only — it loses the Cave subtype [Magus of the Moon ruling #4].
- Abilities: it loses "{T}: Add {C}" and "Other Caves you control have '{T}, Pay 1 life: Add one mana of any color'" and instead has the intrinsic Mountain ability "{T}: Add {R}" [Magus of the Moon ruling #4]. Note {C} (colorless specifically) is no longer available from it; it now produces {R}.
- Name: still Forgotten Monument; Magus of the Moon doesn't change names or supertypes, and changing subtypes never changes supertypes [Magus of the Moon ruling #1, 205.4b].
- Since Forgotten Monument is no longer a Cave and no longer grants its ability, any other Caves Alex controls also lose that granted mana ability (and they too are Mountains).

Meanwhile Magus of the Moon itself is a green Lizard creature with base power and toughness 4/4 and no abilities, and that effect doesn't wear off at end of turn [Lizard, Connors's Curse ruling #0].

This analysis doesn't depend on the number of players; it works the same in two-player and multiplayer games, since Magus of the Moon affects all nonbasic lands regardless of controller.

question: Ainsley enchants their [Colossus Hammer] with [Rune of Flight]. Then they equip it to [Skeletal Snake]. Does Skeletal Snake have flying?
answer:
Yes — Skeletal Snake has flying (and is 12/11).

This is exactly the example in the timestamp rules. Rune of Flight says "As long as enchanted permanent is an Equipment, it has 'Equipped creature has flying,'" so Colossus Hammer now has two relevant abilities: its own "Equipped creature gets +10/+10 and loses flying" and the granted "Equipped creature has flying." The granted ability takes Rune of Flight's timestamp, since that's later than Colossus Hammer's timestamp [613.7a].

When Colossus Hammer becomes attached to Skeletal Snake, it receives a new timestamp [613.7e], and both of its abilities receive new timestamps — but their relative order is unchanged [613.7a]. So the order is still: (1) Colossus Hammer's own "loses flying," then (2) the Rune of Flight-granted "has flying." One continuous effect overriding another in layer 6 is settled by timestamp order, and the later effect wins [613.9]. The later effect grants flying, so Skeletal Snake ends up with flying.

Note also that Skeletal Snake had no flying to begin with, which doesn't matter — Colossus Hammer can be attached to a non-flier, it just has nothing to remove [Colossus Hammer ruling #0], and a creature that gains flying after Colossus Hammer is attached keeps it [Colossus Hammer ruling #2]. Skeletal Snake also still gets +10/+10 from Colossus Hammer, since that part isn't overridden, making it a 12/11 flier. Skeletal Snake counts as modified, being equipped [700.9].

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Rune of Flight was attached to Colossus Hammer before Colossus Hammer was equipped, as stated. If instead Colossus Hammer were already attached to Skeletal Snake and Rune of Flight were then put onto Colossus Hammer, the granted flying ability would still have the later timestamp and Skeletal Snake would still have flying. The reverse case — attaching Rune of Flight first, then later re-equipping — also keeps flying, per rule 613.7a. Player count is irrelevant here; the answer is the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

question: Ashley equips [Colossus Hammer] to [Ogre Warrior], then enchants it with [Phantom Wings]. Does Ogre Warrior have flying?
answer:
Yes — Ogre Warrior has flying (and is 13/13).

Both Colossus Hammer's "loses flying" and Phantom Wings' "Enchanted creature has flying" are continuous effects applying in the same layer, and neither depends on the other, so they're applied in timestamp order and the later one wins [613.9]. Colossus Hammer became attached first (getting its timestamp when it was attached [613.7e]); Phantom Wings entered the battlefield attached afterward, so its grant of flying has the later timestamp and overrides Colossus Hammer's removal [613.7a][613.9]. This matches the Colossus Hammer ruling that a creature which gains flying after Colossus Hammer became attached keeps that flying [Colossus Hammer ruling #2].

Colossus Hammer still gives +10/+10, so Ogre Warrior is a 13/13 flier. Note the ability comes from Phantom Wings' static ability and applies as long as Phantom Wings stays attached to Ogre Warrior [604.4].

If the order were reversed — Phantom Wings attached first, then Colossus Hammer equipped — Colossus Hammer would have the later timestamp and Ogre Warrior would not have flying.

Nothing here depends on the number of players; the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

question: Ari controls [Magus of the Moon] enchanted with [Ichthyomorphosis]. Is Ari's [Dormant Volcano] a Mountain?
answer:
Yes. Ari's Dormant Volcano is still a Mountain. Ichthyomorphosis makes the enchanted creature "lose all abilities," but a specific ruling covers exactly this: if Magus of the Moon loses its abilities, it continues to turn nonbasic lands into Mountains, because effects that change subtypes are applied before effects that remove abilities, regardless of the order in which those effects began [Magus of the Moon ruling #0]. So Magus of the Moon (now a 0/1 blue Fish with no abilities) still applies its type-changing effect.

Consequences for Dormant Volcano, a nonbasic land: it loses its other land types and all of its own abilities — including "This land enters tapped," the enter-the-battlefield sacrifice trigger, and "{T}: Add {C}{R}" — and instead has the land type Mountain with the intrinsic ability "{T}: Add {R}" [Magus of the Moon ruling #4], [305.6], [205.3i]. Note it can no longer produce {C} (colorless mana specifically); it taps only for {R}.

It does not become a basic land, and its name is still Dormant Volcano, not "Mountain" — Magus of the Moon doesn't affect names or supertypes [Magus of the Moon ruling #1].

This answer doesn't depend on player count; Magus of the Moon affects all nonbasic lands, so with more than two players every opponent's nonbasic lands are Mountains too, exactly as in a two-player game.

question: Averie controls [Muraganda Petroglyphs] and [Wayward Angel], and has more than 7 cards in their graveyard. Nathan casts and resolves [Humility]. What are Wayward Angel's characteristics?
answer:
Wayward Angel ends up a 3/3 black Angel Horror creature with no abilities (name Wayward Angel, mana cost {4}{W}{W}, so MV 6).

How it gets there, layer by layer (613.1f, 613.1g, 613.4a–c, 613.7):

- Color (applied before ability-removal): Wayward Angel's Threshold ability still exists when color-changing effects are applied, and with seven or more cards in Averie's graveyard it makes Wayward Angel black instead of white — it is black, not white and black [Wayward Angel ruling #0].
- Layer 6 (ability-adding/removing, 613.1f): In timestamp order, Wayward Angel's Threshold ability would grant trample and the "At the beginning of your upkeep, sacrifice a creature" trigger, but Humility has the later timestamp and removes all abilities from all creatures. Result: Wayward Angel has no abilities at all (no flying, no vigilance, no trample, and its own Threshold ability is gone).
- Layer 7b (613.4b): Humility sets Wayward Angel's base power and toughness to 1/1, replacing the printed 4/4.

question: Nico controls [Urza's Saga] with two lore counters on it. Alexzander uses [Jinx] to change its land type. What happens?
answer:
Urza's Saga becomes a basic land type of Alexzander's choice (say Island) until end of turn, loses its chapter abilities, and — per its own ruling — Nico immediately sacrifices it. It does keep the abilities chapters I and II already granted it, but only for the instant before it's sacrificed.

Details:

1. Jinx sets the land's subtype to a basic land type. Under [305.7], when an effect sets a land's subtype to a basic land type, the land loses its old land types and all abilities generated from its rules text, and gains the mana ability for the new basic type (so it taps for that color). The chapter abilities I, II, and III are printed rules-text abilities of Urza's Saga ([107.15a], [714.2b] — a chapter symbol is a keyword ability representing a triggered ability), so they are stripped.
2. [305.7] also says this does not remove abilities granted by other effects, and it doesn't change card types or supertypes ([205.4b]). So Urza's Saga is still an Enchantment Land and still a Saga subtype, and it keeps "{T}: Add {C}" and "{2}, {T}: Create a 0/0 colorless Construct..." that chapters I and II gave it ([Urza's Saga ruling #5]).
3. Because Urza's Saga is now a Saga with no chapter abilities, [Urza's Saga ruling #1] states directly that it will immediately be sacrificed (that ruling covers exactly this case — losing all chapter abilities while remaining a Saga, e.g. via Blood Moon). Note the general state-based action in [704.5s]/[714.4] is worded to apply to a Saga "with one or more chapter abilities"; the card-specific ruling is the authoritative answer here, so treat Urza's Saga as sacrificed as a state-based action, without using the stack.

Practical upshot for Nico: the two lore counters no longer matter, chapter III never triggers, so Nico gets no artifact tutor. If Nico wants value, they should activate the Construct-token ability (with {2} and tapping) before Jinx resolves, since once Jinx resolves Urza's Saga is sacrificed immediately and the token ability can't be used.

Timing note: I'm assuming Jinx resolves while Urza's Saga has only two lore counters, as stated. If instead the third lore counter had already been put on and chapter III had triggered, Urza's Saga would already be waiting to be sacrificed once that chapter ability left the stack ([714.4], [Urza's Saga ruling #4]), and Jinx would only strip a chapter ability that no longer matters — the already-triggered chapter III on the stack would still resolve.

This interaction doesn't depend on player count: it plays out the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table, since only Nico's own Saga and Alexzander's instant are involved.

question: Aaden activates [Inkmoth Nexus], equips [Colossus Hammer] to it, then activates Inkmoth Nexus again. What are the characteristics of Inkmoth Nexus?
answer:
Inkmoth Nexus ends up an 11/11 Phyrexian Blinkmoth artifact creature land with flying and infect (and it's still a land, colorless, named Inkmoth Nexus).

How that resolves:

- Power/toughness: Both activations of Inkmoth Nexus set its power and toughness to 1/1. Two effects setting the same characteristic are applied in timestamp order, so the second activation's 1/1 simply overwrites the first's 1/1 (no change) [613.7]. Colossus Hammer's "+10/+10" is a modification applied after characteristic-setting effects, giving 11/11.
- Types: Each activation of Inkmoth Nexus makes it an artifact creature with the types Phyrexian Blinkmoth and specifies "It's still a land," so Inkmoth Nexus is a Land Artifact Creature — Phyrexian Blinkmoth. Colossus Hammer doesn't change types.
- Flying: This is the interesting part. Colossus Hammer says the equipped creature "loses flying," while the second activation of Inkmoth Nexus grants flying. Both are ability-adding/removing effects applied in timestamp order [613.7], [613.7a]. Colossus Hammer's timestamp is when it became attached to Inkmoth Nexus [613.7e]; the second activation of Inkmoth Nexus resolved after that, so it has the later timestamp. Applying them in order: Colossus Hammer removes the flying granted by the first activation, then the second activation grants flying again. Net result: Inkmoth Nexus has flying. (If instead Colossus Hammer had been attached — or re-attached, which gives it a new timestamp — after the second activation, Inkmoth Nexus would not have flying.)
- Infect: Granted by both activations, untouched by Colossus Hammer, so Inkmoth Nexus has infect and deals its damage as -1/-1 counters to creatures and poison counters to players.

Timing assumption: I'm reading the sequence exactly as stated — activate, then equip, then activate again, with each effect resolving before the next action. All of this is independent of player count; nothing here differs between a two-player and a multiplayer game.

One practical note: per Inkmoth Nexus's rulings, it can only attack (or be tapped for mana while a creature) if you've controlled it continuously since your most recent turn began [Inkmoth Nexus ruling #1], [Inkmoth Nexus ruling #0].

question: Alvin controls [Mycosynth Lattice], a [Dance of the Dead] attached to a [Streetbreaker Wurm] that it returned to the battlefield, and a [Mizzium Transreliquat] that is currently a copy of [Sakashima of a Thousand Faces] due to its second ability. Alvin casts [Eureka], choosing to put [March of the Machines] onto the battlefield, then putting [Copy Artifact] onto the battlefield, which copies the Mizzium Transreliquat and then copies the Dance of the Dead with its new copy ability. (The one from Sakashima of a Thousand Faces.) They choose for it to enchant a [Viashino Warrior] in their graveyard. As Eureka continues resolving, they put [Shimatsu the Bloodcloaked] onto the battlefield and sacrifice March of the Machines. After Copy Artifact's trigger resolves and returns the Viashino Warrior to the battlefield, Alvin activates the ability of the Copy Artifact to turn it into a copy of Streetbreaker Wurm. What happens?
answer:
**Direct answer:** The Copy Artifact stops being a Dance of the Dead and becomes a 6/4 Wurm named Streetbreaker Wurm (still with the {1}{U}{R} Mizzium Transreliquat ability). Because it never left the battlefield, its "When this Aura leaves the battlefield, that creature's controller sacrifices it" trigger never triggers — the Viashino Warrior that the Copy Artifact returned stays on the battlefield permanently. The Viashino Warrior also loses the +1/+1 and the "doesn't untap during its controller's untap step" restriction, so it is a plain 4/2 that is still tapped (status is retained, 110.5) but will untap normally on Alvin's next untap step.

**How the pieces got there:**

1. The Mizzium Transreliquat's second ability made its copiable values those of Sakashima of a Thousand Faces plus the {1}{U}{R} ability (Mizzium Transreliquat ruling #0). Copy effects are copied, so the Copy Artifact copying the Mizzium Transreliquat gets Sakashima of a Thousand Faces + that ability (707.3, Mizzium Transreliquat ruling #3).
2. Both the Copy Artifact copy effect and the copied Sakashima of a Thousand Faces "enter as a copy" effect are replacement effects applying as the Copy Artifact enters; Alvin orders them (616.1f), applying Copy Artifact's first so the Sakashima ability exists to be used — exactly the Essence of the Wild/Rusted Sentinel pattern in 616.1f. With Mycosynth Lattice plus March of the Machines still on the battlefield, the Dance of the Dead was a noncreature artifact turned into an artifact creature, so it was a legal "another creature you control" for Sakashima's ability (Mycosynth Lattice, March of the Machines).
3. So the Copy Artifact entered as a copy of Dance of the Dead, keeping Sakashima of a Thousand Faces' other abilities including the {1}{U}{R} ability, and Alvin made its own "enchant creature card in a graveyard" choice fresh, picking the Viashino Warrior (707.6).
4. Crucially, an Aura that is also a creature can't enchant anything and is unattached and then put into the graveyard **as state-based actions** (Mycosynth Lattice ruling #3). State-based actions are only checked when a player would receive priority, and Eureka was still resolving; March of the Machines was sacrificed to Shimatsu the Bloodcloaked before Eureka finished. So neither the Copy Artifact nor the original Dance of the Dead was ever checked while it was a creature, and both survive as ordinary Auras.
5. The Copy Artifact's enters trigger then resolved, putting the Viashino Warrior onto the battlefield tapped under Alvin's control and attaching the Copy Artifact to it.

**The activation:** Streetbreaker Wurm is an artifact because of Mycosynth Lattice, so it's a legal target for "{1}{U}{R}: This artifact becomes a copy of target artifact, except it has this ability." The new copy effect overwrites the old one (Mizzium Transreliquat ruling #2), and only Streetbreaker Wurm's copiable values are copied — not Mycosynth Lattice's type change, not the Dance of the Dead's +1/+1, and not counters (707.2). It also loses Sakashima of a Thousand Faces' abilities and the Dance of the Dead text entirely. Noncopy effects still on the permanent would remain (707.4), and it keeps its statuses (110.5, 110.5c). Since it is no longer an Aura, it simply becomes an unattached permanent; it's a creature that entered this turn, so it can't attack this turn absent haste.

**Timing note:** I assumed the order as written — March of the Machines is gone before Eureka finishes resolving, and the Copy Artifact's enters trigger resolves before the {1}{U}{R} activation. If instead a player somehow received priority while both March of the Machines and the Aura-creature Copy Artifact existed, the Copy Artifact (and the original Dance of the Dead) would have been unattached and put into the graveyard by state-based actions, and its leaves-the-battlefield trigger would have forced sacrifice of the enchanted creature.

**Player count:** nothing here depends on the number of players; Eureka's "starting with you, each player" simply involves more players at a multiplayer table, and simultaneous choices would be made in APNAP order (101.4).

question: Ari casts [Aeve, Progenitor Ooze], with two spells having been cast before then. Nadia controls [Humility]. What will Ari's battlefield look like once the stack fully resolves and state-based actions are checked?
answer:
Ari ends up with three Aeve permanents on the battlefield: two Aeve, Progenitor Ooze token copies and the original Aeve, Progenitor Ooze card. All three have no abilities (Humility), and their sizes are 1/1, 2/2, and 3/3 respectively. Nothing dies when state-based actions are checked.

How that happens:

1. Storm: two spells were cast earlier in the turn, so casting Aeve, Progenitor Ooze creates two copies of the spell, which become tokens. The copies resolve first, one at a time, then the original spell resolves [608.1] [Aeve, Progenitor Ooze ruling #2].

2. Counters: "Aeve enters with a +1/+1 counter on it for each other Ooze you control" is applied as each one enters the battlefield. Humility only affects creatures already on the battlefield, so it doesn't strip this ability off a spell still on the stack. Assuming Ari controlled no other Oozes to start, the first token enters with 0 counters, the second with 1, and the original Aeve, Progenitor Ooze with 2 [Aeve, Progenitor Ooze ruling #2].

3. Humility: "All creatures lose all abilities and have base power and toughness 1/1." Losing abilities happens in layer 6; setting base power/toughness happens in layer 7b; +1/+1 counters are applied later in layer 7, after base-setting effects [613.1a] [613.1g] [613.5] [Humility ruling #2]. So base 1/1 plus counters gives 1/1, 2/2, and 3/3. Timestamps don't help here, because counters are applied in a later part of layer 7 than Humility's base-setting effect regardless of order [613.7] [613.8].

4. Legend rule: "Aeve isn't legendary if it's a token" is a supertype-changing effect applied in layer 4, before Humility strips abilities in layer 6, and per Humility ruling #2 such effects still finish applying even though the ability is later lost [Humility ruling #2]. So the two tokens aren't legendary and only the original is, meaning the legend rule doesn't force any sacrifice. Also note Humility strips Aeve's abilities, but not its Ooze creature type, so each new Aeve still counted the earlier ones as Oozes.

5. State-based actions are checked only after each spell finishes resolving, not mid-resolution, and every one of the three has toughness 1 or more, so none is put into the graveyard [704.4].

Timing note: I'm assuming Humility was already on the battlefield before Aeve, Progenitor Ooze was cast and stayed there throughout. If Nadia's Humility left the battlefield before the copies resolved, the Aeves would instead be 2/2 base with their counters (2/2, 3/3, 4/4) and would keep their abilities, and the legend rule would still spare the tokens.

Player count doesn't change anything here: Humility affects all creatures regardless of controller, so the result is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

question: Natalie controls [High Fae Trickster]. Allen activates the crew ability of [Capenna Express]. Before it resolves Natalie casts [One with the Stars] targeting Capenna Express. What happens when the crew ability resolves?
answer:
Direct answer: the crew ability still resolves and does what it says — Capenna Express becomes an artifact creature until end of turn. One with the Stars did not counter or fizzle the ability: crew doesn't target, and the tapping of creatures with total power 3 or more already happened as a cost when Allen activated the ability, so nothing is refunded (702.122a, 702.122b).

Why Natalie could do this at all: High Fae Trickster says "You may cast spells as though they had flash," so Natalie may cast One with the Stars, normally a sorcery-speed Aura, during Allen's turn while the crew ability is on the stack.

Sequence I'm assuming: One with the Stars was cast in response and resolves first, attaching to Capenna Express and making it an enchantment that loses all other card types; then Allen's crew ability resolves. The crew ability's type-changing effect is created later than the Aura's, so for the rest of the turn Capenna Express is an artifact creature (a 6/6) despite the Aura, and Allen can attack with it. Once the "until end of turn" crew effect wears off, One with the Stars's effect reasserts itself: per One with the Stars ruling #1, an Aura that enchanted a permanent that was only temporarily a creature (such as a Vehicle) keeps that permanent an enchantment even after the temporary effect expires. So Capenna Express ends up as a permanent that is only an enchantment (still keeping its abilities), no longer an artifact or creature.

If instead you meant the crew ability somehow resolving before One with the Stars, nothing changes about the crew resolution; the Aura simply applies afterward with the same end result once the until-end-of-turn effect expires.

One caveat: the numbered layer rules that govern which of two conflicting type-changing effects applies weren't included in my context, so the "later effect wins during this turn" part rests on One with the Stars ruling #1 rather than on a quoted layer rule. Nothing here depends on player count — the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

question: Nico controls [Humility]. Aitana casts [Finale of Devastation] with X = 10. Will the creature they find have haste?
answer:
Yes — the creature Aitana finds will have haste (and be 11/11), assuming Nico's Humility was already on the battlefield before Finale of Devastation resolved.

Why: Humility says "All creatures lose all abilities and have base power and toughness 1/1." That ability-removal is a continuous effect that applies in layer 6, and Finale of Devastation's "creatures you control get +X/+X and gain haste until end of turn" also applies in layer 6 (for haste) and layer 7c (for the +10/+10 boost). Two effects in the same layer are applied in timestamp order, and Finale of Devastation's effect has the later timestamp, so it grants haste after Humility has stripped abilities — Humility does not continuously re-remove abilities granted later. The power/toughness math works the same way: Humility sets base 1/1 in layer 7b, then Finale of Devastation's +10/+10 applies in layer 7c, giving 11/11. Finale of Devastation's ruling confirms the creature you just put onto the battlefield does get +X/+X and haste when X is 10 or more, and that no player can act in between [Finale of Devastation ruling #2, Finale of Devastation ruling #0].

Haste means the creature ignores the "summoning sickness" rule: it can attack and can use activated abilities with {T} or untap symbols in the cost even though it hasn't been controlled by Aitana continuously since her most recent turn began [702.10a, 702.10b, 702.10c, 302.6].

Timing caveat: if instead Humility entered the battlefield *after* Finale of Devastation resolved (later timestamp), Humility's ability-removal would apply after the haste grant and the creature would lose haste — though it would still be 11/11, since Humility only sets base power/toughness in layer 7b while the +10/+10 applies in layer 7c [Humility ruling #2].

This analysis doesn't depend on player count: Humility affects all creatures and Finale of Devastation affects only its controller's creatures, so the result is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

question: Avery's [Unlicensed Hearse] has exiled five cards, and they activate its crew ability. After that resolves, Avery casts [Dress Down]. What does Unlicensed Hearse look like?
answer:
Unlicensed Hearse becomes a 0/0 artifact creature Vehicle with no abilities, and it's immediately put into Avery's graveyard as a state-based action (unless something else is boosting its toughness).

Why:
- Crewing does not grant an ability; "Crew 2" resolves as an effect making Unlicensed Hearse an artifact creature until end of turn [702.122a]. Dress Down removes abilities, not creature types, so Unlicensed Hearse stays a creature after Dress Down resolves.
- Unlicensed Hearse's printed power and toughness are */*, and the only thing defining those values is its own ability "Unlicensed Hearse's power and toughness are each equal to the number of cards exiled with it." That is an ability, so Dress Down's "Creatures lose all abilities" strips it (Dress Down only fails to remove abilities granted after it entered [Dress Down ruling #0]).
- With that ability gone, the placeholder * has no effect defining it and is treated as 0 [107.3], so Unlicensed Hearse is 0/0 even though five cards are still exiled with it. A 0-toughness creature is put into its owner's graveyard, exactly as the Vehicle's own ruling describes for an uncrewed-then-crewed 0/0 Hearse [Unlicensed Hearse ruling #0]. It also loses its {T} exile ability and Crew 2 while Dress Down is on the battlefield.
- Timing assumption: you crewed first and Dress Down resolved afterward, as stated. If instead Dress Down were already on the battlefield and you tried to crew, Unlicensed Hearse would have lost Crew 2 and couldn't be crewed at all.
- Note that had Unlicensed Hearse never been crewed, it would be a noncreature permanent with no power or toughness at all [208.3a] and would survive Dress Down.

This interaction involves only Avery's own permanents, so it plays out identically in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table.

It's a 0/0 artifact creature with no abilities. (And will die when state-based actions are checked.)

question:
Alison controls [Mycosynth Lattice], an [Animate Dead] attached to a [Great-Horn Krushok] that it returned to the battlefield, a [Mizzium Transreliquat] that copied [Sakashima of a Thousand Faces] with its second ability, and a [Southern Elephant] enchanted by a [Deep Freeze].

Alison casts [Eureka], choosing to put [March of the Machines] onto the battlefield. Alison then puts [Sculpting Steel] onto the battlefield, choosing to copy the Mizzium Transreliquat and then choosing to copy the Animate Dead with its new copy ability. They choose to enchant a [Gigantosaurus] in their graveyard. As Eureka continues resolving, they put [Shimatsu the Bloodcloaked] onto the battlefield and sacrifice March of the Machines.

After Sculpting Steel's trigger resolves and returns the Gigantosaurus to the battlefield, Alison activates the ability of the Sculpting Steel to turn it into a copy of Deep Freeze. After that resolves, they casts [Enchantment Alteration] to attach it to the Southern Elephant. What happens?
answer:
Bottom line: the Sculpting Steel ends up as a permanent copy of Deep Freeze (still carrying Mizzium Transreliquat's {1}{U}{R} copy ability) attached to Southern Elephant, Southern Elephant is a 0/4 blue Wall artifact creature with defender and no other abilities, and Gigantosaurus stays on the battlefield as a normal 10/10 (artifact, via Mycosynth Lattice) and is NOT sacrificed.

Step by step:

1. Sculpting Steel entering. Sculpting Steel's replacement effect copies Mizzium Transreliquat. Because Mizzium Transreliquat had used its second ability, its copiable values are those of Sakashima of a Thousand Faces plus the granted "{1}{U}{R}: ...except it has this ability" (707.9a, 613.1a, Sculpting Steel ruling #4, Mizzium Transreliquat ruling #3, Sakashima of a Thousand Faces ruling #0). That includes Sakashima of a Thousand Faces' own "enter as a copy of another creature you control" replacement effect, so Alison applies a second copy effect and Sculpting Steel enters as a copy of Animate Dead. Animate Dead was a legal choice only because Mycosynth Lattice made it an artifact and March of the Machines made that noncreature artifact into a creature at that moment.

2. Timing assumption: March of the Machines was sacrificed to Shimatsu the Bloodcloaked later in the same resolution of Eureka, before any player would receive priority. That matters, because while March of the Machines and Mycosynth Lattice are both out, an Aura that is also a creature can't enchant anything and would be unattached and then put into its owner's graveyard as state-based actions (Mycosynth Lattice ruling #3). Since state-based actions aren't checked mid-resolution, and March of the Machines is gone by the time Eureka finishes, both Animate Dead and the new Aura survive attached. If instead March of the Machines had still been on the battlefield when priority came back, every Aura here (Animate Dead, Deep Freeze, and the Sculpting Steel copy) would have been unattached and put into its owner's graveyard.

3. The copied Animate Dead trigger resolves, returning Gigantosaurus to the battlefield and attaching Sculpting Steel (as Animate Dead) to it; Gigantosaurus is 9/10 from the -1/-0 at that point.

4. Activating the {1}{U}{R} ability targeting Deep Freeze. Deep Freeze is a legal target because Mycosynth Lattice makes all permanents artifacts. Sculpting Steel becomes a copy of Deep Freeze, except it keeps that copy ability. This change happens while it stays on the battlefield, so no enters/leaves-the-battlefield abilities trigger and non-copy effects continue (707.4). Crucially, it no longer has Animate Dead's "When this Aura leaves the battlefield, that creature's controller sacrifices it" ability — the copy effect overwrote its text. Its enchant ability is now "enchant creature," and Gigantosaurus is a creature, so it remains legally attached. Because this came from the second (non-"until end of turn") ability, it does not wear off at end of turn (Mizzium Transreliquat ruling #2). Gigantosaurus becomes base 0/4, a blue Wall with defender, and loses all other abilities.

5. Enchantment Alteration moves the Aura from Gigantosaurus (a creature) to Southern Elephant (another creature), which is legal, and the Aura gets a new timestamp (701.3c). Gigantosaurus is left unenchanted: back to 10/10 Dinosaur (still an artifact from Mycosynth Lattice) and it is not sacrificed, since the Animate Dead sacrifice ability no longer exists anywhere.

6. Southern Elephant now has two Deep Freeze effects on it (the original Deep Freeze and the copy). The later-timestamped one overwrites the earlier base-P/T setting, but they set the same values (Deep Freeze ruling #2), so Southern Elephant is a 0/4 blue Wall (plus artifact from Mycosynth Lattice) with defender and no other abilities.

Player count: nothing here changes between two players and multiplayer, except that Eureka lets every player put permanents onto the battlefield and simultaneous choices would be made in APNAP order (101.4); with more opponents, more permanents could enter during that resolution.

answer_gold: Sculpting Steel still has the ability "enchant creature put onto the battlefield with Animate Dead". It does not become attached to Southern Elephant.

question: Alex controls [Karametra, God of Harvests], and then casts [Opalescence]. Their devotion to white is 2. Is Karametra, God of Harvests a creature? If so, what is its power and toughness?
answer:
Yes — Karametra, God of Harvests is a creature, and it's 5/5.

Why: Both Karametra, God of Harvests' own ability ("As long as your devotion to green and white is less than seven, Karametra isn't a creature") and Opalescence's ability ("Each other non-Aura enchantment is a creature in addition to its other types...") are type-changing continuous effects, so both apply in layer 4, in timestamp order (rules 613.1, 613.7, and see Opalescence ruling #3, which confirms the type change happens in layer 4 and the base power/toughness setting happens later, in layer 7b).

Devotion here is low: devotion to green and white counts green and/or white mana symbols in the mana costs of permanents you control (rule 700.5a). Karametra, God of Harvests' cost {3}{G}{W} contributes 2 ({G} and {W}; the {3} is generic and doesn't count), and Opalescence's cost {2}{W}{W} contributes 2. So with just these permanents, devotion to green and white is 4, which is less than seven — Karametra, God of Harvests' own ability would strip its creature type (Karametra ruling #15).

But Opalescence entered later, so its layer‑4 effect is applied after Karametra, God of Harvests' effect and makes Karametra, God of Harvests a creature (in addition to being a legendary enchantment). Then in layer 7b Opalescence sets its base power and base toughness each equal to its mana value; Karametra, God of Harvests' mana value is 5 ({3}{G}{W}), so it is 5/5 — not its printed 6/7, because a base-P/T-setting effect overrides the printed values (rules 208.4b, 208.1, and the Base Power/Base Toughness glossary entry).

Timing note: this answer assumes Karametra, God of Harvests has the earlier timestamp (it was already on the battlefield, as stated). If Opalescence had the earlier timestamp, Karametra, God of Harvests' own ability would be applied last in layer 4 and it would not be a creature (and, having no creature type, would have no power or toughness per rules 208.3 and 302.4) — though Opalescence would still set base P/T in layer 7b, that's irrelevant while it isn't a creature.

Nothing here depends on player count; devotion and layers work the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

question: Autumn animates [Inkmoth Nexus] and attacks with it. Nayeli then flashes in [Dress Down]. What does Inkmoth Nexus look like?
answer:
Inkmoth Nexus remains a 1/1 Phyrexian Blinkmoth artifact creature land that is still attacking, but with no abilities at all — no flying, no infect, and no mana ability. It therefore deals normal combat damage (not poison counters), and it loses evasion, so it can be blocked by creatures without flying/reach (blockers must have been declared legally at the time, though — if blockers were already declared, Dress Down doesn't undo that).

Why: characteristics are determined by starting with the printed card and then applying continuous effects in a series of layers [613.1]. The resolved ability of Inkmoth Nexus sets its types (artifact creature Phyrexian Blinkmoth, still a land) and its power/toughness of 1/1; those are separate from the ability-granting part. Dress Down's "Creatures lose all abilities" strips the granted flying and infect, and also strips Inkmoth Nexus's own printed abilities ({T}: Add {C} and {1}: animate), but it does not undo the type change or the 1/1 power/toughness that the earlier resolution already established [Dress Down, Inkmoth Nexus].

Timing note: I'm assuming Nayeli casts Dress Down after Inkmoth Nexus was animated and declared as an attacker, and that Dress Down resolves before combat damage. Under that assumption, damage is dealt as normal damage to the defending player rather than as poison counters. If Dress Down instead resolved before Autumn activated the animation, Inkmoth Nexus would have lost its {1} animation ability and couldn't have become a creature or attacked at all; if it resolved after combat damage, the poison counters would already have been dealt.

Player count: nothing here changes between a two-player game and a multiplayer table, except that in multiplayer the damage (poison or normal) goes to whichever defending player or planeswalker/battle Inkmoth Nexus was attacking.

question: Aaron equips [Skullclamp] onto [Champion of the Flame]. Does Champion of the Flame die?
answer:
No — Champion of the Flame survives. With Skullclamp attached, Champion of the Flame counts one Equipment attached to it, so its own ability gives it +2/+2 (1/1 becomes 3/3), and Skullclamp's "Equipped creature gets +1/-1" makes it a 4/2. Toughness 2 is greater than 0, so the state-based action that puts a creature with toughness 0 or less into its owner's graveyard [704.5f] never applies, and Skullclamp's "Whenever equipped creature dies, draw two cards" doesn't trigger.

Both static effects apply simultaneously and continuously — there's no moment where Skullclamp's -1 is applied to a 1/1 before Champion of the Flame's own +2/+2 counts the Equipment. Attaching Skullclamp with Equip {1} is what normally kills 1/1 creatures, but Champion of the Flame's printed ability counting Equipment attached to it means it grows instead.

One caution: if Champion of the Flame already has damage marked on it this turn, or if Skullclamp later leaves the battlefield or moves to another creature, Champion of the Flame loses that +2/+2 and the previously nonlethal damage can become lethal [Champion of the Flame ruling #0]. Also, if Champion of the Flame has 2 or more damage marked at the moment Skullclamp becomes attached, that damage is lethal against toughness 2 and it would die then. Nothing here depends on player count, so the answer is the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.613.5: The application of continuous effects as described by the layer system is continually and automatically performed by the game. All resulting changes to an object’s characteristics are instantaneous. Honor of the Pure is an enchantment that reads “White creatures you control get +1/+1.” Honor of the Pure and a 2/2 black creature are on the battlefield under your control. If an effect then turns the creature white (layer 5), it gets +1/+1 from Honor of the Pure (layer 7c), becoming 3/3. If the creature’s color is later changed to red (layer 5), Honor of the Pure’s effect stops applying to it, and it will return to being 2/2. Gray Ogre, a 2/2 creature, is on the battlefield. An effect puts a +1/+1 counter on it (layer 7c), making it 3/3. A spell targeting it that says “Target creature gets +4/+4 until end of turn” resolves (layer 7c), making it 7/7. An enchantment that says “Creatures you control get +0/+2” enters the battlefield (layer 7c), making it 7/9. An effect that says “Target creature becomes 0/1 until end of turn” is applied to it (layer 7b), making it 5/8 (0/1, with +4/+4 from the resolved spell, +0/+2 from the enchantment, and +1/+1 from the counter).
gold_text.704.3: Whenever a player would get priority (see rule 117, “Timing and Priority”), the game checks for any of the listed conditions for state-based actions, then performs all applicable state-based actions simultaneously as a single event. If any state-based actions are performed as a result of a check, the check is repeated; otherwise all triggered abilities that are waiting to be put on the stack are put on the stack, then the check is repeated. Once no more state-based actions have been performed as the result of a check and no triggered abilities are waiting to be put on the stack, the appropriate player gets priority. This process also occurs during the cleanup step (see rule 514), except that if no state-based actions are performed as the result of the step’s first check and no triggered abilities are waiting to be put on the stack, then no player gets priority and the step ends.

answer_gold: No, Champion of the Flame will be a 4/2 and not die. All continuous effects are applied instantly before state based actions are checked.

question: In their first main phase, Alexandra activates [Sokenzan, Crucible of Defiance] to create two tokens, and Nehemiah responds with [Dress Down]. What happens with the tokens?
answer:
The two tokens are still created, and they still have haste. Nehemiah's Dress Down doesn't stop tokens from being created and doesn't strip the haste in this case.

Why: Alexandra's Channel ability from Sokenzan, Crucible of Defiance is already on the stack when Nehemiah casts Dress Down with flash, so Dress Down is on top and resolves first (rule 608.1). Dress Down then sets up its continuous "Creatures lose all abilities" effect. When Alexandra's Sokenzan, Crucible of Defiance ability afterward resolves, it puts two 1/1 colorless Spirit creature tokens onto the battlefield (rule 701.7a). Nothing about Dress Down says a permanent with those characteristics can't enter the battlefield, so rule 111.5 (the only rule that stops token creation for that reason) doesn't apply — the tokens exist.

The haste survives because the same resolution of Sokenzan, Crucible of Defiance's ability grants haste after Dress Down is already on the battlefield. Per Dress Down ruling #0, an ability granted to a creature after Dress Down has entered isn't lost; Dress Down only removes abilities the creature already had. The Spirit tokens have no printed abilities of their own to lose, so the net result is two 1/1 colorless Spirits with haste that can attack this turn.

Assumed timing: Nehemiah cast Dress Down in response to the activated ability, so Dress Down resolves first. If instead Dress Down had somehow already resolved and then the tokens were created — that's the same outcome here. The only case where the tokens would lose haste is if the haste grant happened before Dress Down entered the battlefield (i.e., Dress Down cast after the Channel ability fully resolved); then the tokens would lose haste, though they'd remain on the battlefield as 1/1 Spirits.

Dress Down also triggers its own "draw a card" for Nehemiah, and it is sacrificed at the beginning of the end step; the tokens remain on the battlefield after that (they only cease to exist if they leave the battlefield, per rules 111.7 and 704.5d). None of this depends on the number of players — the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

question: Aubree casts [Blood Moon]. Nikolas activates [Inkmoth Nexus]'s ability in response. What will Inkmoth Nexus look like after everything resolves? What will it look like next turn?
answer:
Direct answer: After both resolve, Inkmoth Nexus is a 1/1 artifact creature that is a Mountain (plus its Phyrexian Blinkmoth creature types) with only the ability "{T}: Add {R}" — it loses flying, infect, its "{T}: Add {C}" ability and its own {1} animation ability. Next turn, the animation effect has worn off, so it's just a nonbasic land that is a Mountain with "{T}: Add {R}" — no power/toughness, not a creature, no flying/infect, no {C}.

Timing assumption: Nikolas activated Inkmoth Nexus's ability while Blood Moon was still on the stack, so the animation ability resolves first and Blood Moon resolves second, giving Blood Moon the later timestamp. (If instead Blood Moon had already resolved first, Inkmoth Nexus would have lost its {1} ability and couldn't have been activated at all — see Blood Moon ruling #2.)

Why: characteristics are recalculated in layers (rule 613.1d), and a single effect applies its parts in each applicable layer (rule 613.6). In layer 4, Inkmoth Nexus's own effect makes it an artifact creature Blinkmoth (Phyrexian) that's still a land; then Blood Moon, with the later timestamp, sets its land types to Mountain and strips its land abilities, granting "{T}: Add {R}" (Blood Moon ruling #2). Blood Moon doesn't remove the artifact/creature types or the creature types Phyrexian Blinkmoth, and it doesn't change its name (Blood Moon ruling #1) — it's still named Inkmoth Nexus. Because Blood Moon's ability-removing effect has the later timestamp, the flying and infect granted by the earlier-resolving activated ability are also gone. The power/toughness-setting part still applies, so it is 1/1.

Practical notes: it can attack this turn only if Nikolas has controlled it continuously since his most recent turn began (Inkmoth Nexus ruling #1); if it entered this turn, it can neither attack nor be tapped for mana while it's a creature (Inkmoth Nexus ruling #0). It taps for {R}, not {C}, while Blood Moon is out.

This analysis doesn't depend on the number of players; it is the same at a two-player or multiplayer table.

question: Niko controls [Urza's Saga] on chapter 2. Ainsley casts [Magus of the Moon]. What happens to Urza's Saga?
answer:
Urza's Saga is put into Niko's graveyard immediately — Niko sacrifices it as soon as Magus of the Moon resolves, even though it only has 2 lore counters.

Why: Magus of the Moon says "Nonbasic lands are Mountains." That sets Urza's Saga's land subtypes to just Mountain, which removes the abilities it had from its land types and its chapter abilities, but it does not remove the enchantment subtype Saga. Urza's Saga's own ruling covers exactly this: if Urza's Saga loses all of its chapter abilities but is still a Saga, it is immediately sacrificed [Urza's Saga ruling #1]. That sacrifice is a state-based action, so it happens as soon as a player would receive priority and doesn't use the stack [704.5s], [714.4].

Two notes:
- Any ability Urza's Saga already gained from chapter I or chapter II (the {T}: Add {C} ability and the {2}, {T}: make a Construct ability) is also gone once Magus of the Moon overwrites its land types — and in any case the permanent is sacrificed right away, so Niko can't activate the Construct ability afterward. If Niko wants a Construct token, he must activate that ability while Magus of the Moon is still a spell on the stack, before it resolves (holding priority), since it will be too late once Magus of the Moon resolves [Urza's Saga ruling #5].
- Chapter III never triggers, because Urza's Saga leaves the battlefield before it ever reaches 3 lore counters (lore counters are added as a turn-based action at the start of Niko's precombat main phase) [714.3c], [505.4], [714.2b].

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Magus of the Moon fully resolves while Urza's Saga is on the battlefield with 2 lore counters and no chapter ability of it is on the stack. If a chapter ability of Urza's Saga had triggered and were still on the stack, the state-based check would wait until that ability left the stack [714.4].

Multiplayer: this is the same regardless of player count — Magus of the Moon affects all nonbasic lands, so every player's Urza's Saga is sacrificed by its own controller, not just Niko's.

question: Ariana controls [Painter's Servant] naming "blue." Nico casts [Dress Down]. What color are Painter's Servant and Dress Down?
answer:
After Dress Down resolves: Painter's Servant is colorless, and Dress Down is blue.

Why:

1. Dress Down says "Creatures lose all abilities." Painter's Servant is an Artifact Creature — Scarecrow, so it loses both "As this creature enters, choose a color" and the static ability "All cards that aren't on the battlefield, spells, and permanents are the chosen color in addition to their other colors." With that static ability gone, nothing is adding blue to anything anymore.

2. Painter's Servant's mana cost is {2} — entirely generic mana, no colored symbols — so by rule 202.2a an object with a mana cost of {2} is colorless, and it has no color indicator (204.2) or color-defining characteristic-defining ability (105.2, 604.3) left to change that. So Painter's Servant is colorless.

3. Dress Down's mana cost is {1}{U}: one generic mana plus one blue mana. The {U} makes it blue (202.2a, 202.2f), and Dress Down doesn't remove its own or any enchantment's abilities, only creatures'. So Dress Down is mono-blue.

Timing note: I'm assuming you're asking about the state after Dress Down has resolved. Before that — while Dress Down is still a spell on the stack — Painter's Servant's ability is intact, so it applies to spells and permanents: Painter's Servant itself would be blue (a normally colorless object simply becomes the chosen color rather than being blue and colorless, per Painter's Servant ruling #0), and Dress Down would be blue in addition to its other colors, which is still just blue since blue was chosen (Painter's Servant ruling #5). So the visible change on resolution is only to Painter's Servant, which goes from blue to colorless.

Also note that a genuine color-changing effect would overwrite Painter's Servant's added color (105.3, 613.1e layer 5, Painter's Servant ruling #4), but Dress Down isn't such an effect — it works by stripping the ability itself.

This answer is the same whether the game has two players or more; nothing here depends on player count, and Painter's Servant affects all cards, spells, and permanents regardless of controller.

question: Anabella controls [Blood Moon] and enchants their [Sunlit Marsh] with [Urban Utopia]. What colors can it tap for?
answer:
Sunlit Marsh can tap for any one color — white, blue, black, red, or green — using the ability granted by Urban Utopia, and it also has "{T}: Add {R}" from Blood Moon. What it can no longer do is produce {W} or {B} from its own printed Plains Swamp typeline abilities, because Blood Moon stripped those.

How that happens:
- Sunlit Marsh is a nonbasic land (Blood Moon ruling #1: Blood Moon doesn't make lands basic and doesn't change names), so Blood Moon applies to it. Blood Moon ruling #2: it loses its other land types (Plains, Swamp) and all its abilities, becomes a Mountain, and gains "{T}: Add {R}" — the Mountain type intrinsically grants that ability anyway ([Mountain], [305.6]).
- Urban Utopia grants the enchanted land "{T}: Add one mana of any color." Since the Aura was put onto Sunlit Marsh after Blood Moon was already applying (the timing I'm assuming from the question's order), its ability-granting effect has the later timestamp and is applied after Blood Moon's ability-removal, so the granted mana ability sticks. Urban Utopia ruling #0 also confirms Urban Utopia doesn't change the land's types, so Sunlit Marsh stays a Mountain.
- "Any color" means one of the five colors: white, blue, black, red, or green ([105.1], [107.4a]). Each activation produces one mana of a single color you choose; it is not colorless mana ({C}) and not generic.

Timing caveat: if instead Urban Utopia had been attached first and Blood Moon entered afterward, Blood Moon's later timestamp would remove the granted "{T}: Add one mana of any color" ability too, leaving Sunlit Marsh able to produce only {R}.

Nothing here depends on the number of players, so the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

question: Avery enchants their [Hall] with [Unbridled Growth]. Next turn, Nickolas casts [Blood Moon]. What colors of mana can Hall tap for?
answer:
Hall can tap only for {R} (red).

Why: Blood Moon says "Nonbasic lands are Mountains." Hall is a nonbasic land, so Blood Moon makes it a Mountain, and per the Blood Moon ruling, nonbasic lands lose any other land types and abilities they had and gain the land type Mountain plus the ability "{T}: Add {R}" [Blood Moon ruling #2], [305.6]. Because Nickolas cast Blood Moon after Unbridled Growth was already attached, Blood Moon's ability‑removing effect has the later timestamp and so also strips the "{T}: Add one mana of any color" ability that Unbridled Growth granted to Hall, as well as Hall's own "{T}: Add {R} or {W}" and its "{4}, {T}: Investigate" ability. What's left is the Mountain's intrinsic red mana ability, and {R} is red mana specifically, not generic or colorless [107.4a], [106.1a].

Note that Unbridled Growth itself is unaffected as a permanent — it stays attached and Avery can still sacrifice it to draw a card; it just isn't granting Hall any usable mana ability while Blood Moon is on the battlefield. Had Unbridled Growth instead entered after Blood Moon resolved, its later timestamp would let it grant "{T}: Add one mana of any color," and Hall could then tap for any one of the five colors ({W}, {U}, {B}, {R}, or {G}) [105.1].

The number of players doesn't matter here: Blood Moon affects all nonbasic lands regardless of who controls them, so the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

question: What layer does [Grand Abolisher]'s "During your turn, your opponents can't cast spells or activate abilities of artifacts, creatures, or enchantments." ability apply in?
answer:
Grand Abolisher's ability doesn't apply in any of the layers at all. The layer system of rule 613 exists only to determine the values of an object's characteristics — continuous effects that change copiable values (layer 1), control (layer 2), abilities (layer 6), and so on [613.1, 613.1a, 613.1b, 613.1f]. Grand Abolisher's ability changes no characteristic of any object; it is a static ability that generates a continuous effect stating that something can't happen (your opponents can't cast spells or activate abilities of artifacts, creatures, or enchantments during your turn). Effects that say something can't happen aren't characteristic-modifying effects and aren't replacement effects either; they simply prohibit the action [614.17], and a player can't begin to activate an ability that's prohibited from being activated [602.5].

So there's no timestamp or dependency question to resolve for Grand Abolisher within a layer [613.3, 613.7, 613.8] — it just applies as a restriction whenever an opponent tries to cast a spell or activate a qualifying ability during your turn.

Two notes on scope from the card's own rulings: Grand Abolisher does not stop triggered or static abilities [Grand Abolisher ruling #0], and it does not stop activated abilities of artifact, creature, or enchantment cards in zones other than the battlefield, such as cycling from hand [Grand Abolisher ruling #1].

This works the same in two-player and multiplayer games: the card says "your opponents," so at a multiplayer table it restricts every opponent, not just one, during each of your turns.
